highlight: Wallachia to the old Moldavian capital: Romania’s busiest eastern corridor, hours of steppe and vineyards ending in university-city Iași.

name: ITX-Maum · Donghae Line
highlight: Korea’s newest line: the last east-coast gap closed on New Year’s Day 2025, and now one train runs the whole East Sea shore, Busan to Gangneung.

name: Güney Kurtalan Ekspresi
highlight: The third of Turkey’s great eastern sleepers: off the Anatolian plateau to Diyarbakır’s black basalt walls and the Tigris, ending at railhead Kurtalan.

name: Limited Express Shinano
highlight: Tilting up the Kiso Valley: the old Nakasendō post road’s gorge and pass country on the classic mountain road to Nagano.

name: Limited Express Kuroshio
highlight: Around the Kii Peninsula with the Pacific at the window: Shirahama’s sands, Honshu’s southernmost cape and the Kumano pilgrim coast.

name: Limited Express Nanpu
highlight: Across the Great Seto Bridge, then up the Yoshino river’s Oboke and Koboke gorges, tilting over the island spine to Kochi.

name: Toros Ekspresi
highlight: Heir to the Taurus Express of Agatha Christie fame: down the Cilician Gates on Baghdad Railway engineering to the cotton plains of Adana.

name: IRN Corona
highlight: Romania’s classic night loop: asleep through Székely Land and the Maramureș foothills, waking at the far northwestern corner of the country.

name: Limited Express Shiokaze
highlight: Along the Seto Inland Sea’s island-studded shore to Dōgo Onsen, Japan’s oldest hot spring. Shikoku’s busiest express, tilting the whole way.

name: KTX Jeolla Line
highlight: Off the Honam high-speed line at Iksan and down the Jeolla branch: hanok-roofed Jeonju, Suncheon’s gardens and the Expo harbour at Yeosu.

name: BDZ Fast Train
highlight: Capital to the Danube: through the Iskar gorge, across the Pleven plain, down to Ruse’s Habsburg-flavoured riverfront and the bridge to Romania.

name: InterRegio
highlight: The Moldavia main line north through Bacău and Roman to Suceava, jumping-off point for Bukovina’s painted monasteries.

name: Limited Express Kamui
highlight: Hokkaido’s busiest shuttle: near-hourly across the Ishikari plain to Asahikawa, the doorway to Biei’s hills and Daisetsuzan’s peaks.

name: Limited Express Okhotsk
highlight: One of Japan’s last great remote expresses: over the Kitami Pass through forest-empty interior to the drift-ice coast of the Sea of Okhotsk.

name: Limited Express Sōya
highlight: One return working a day to Japan’s northernmost station: five hours up the Sōya Main Line to Wakkanai, in sight of Sakhalin on a clear day.

name: Missouri River Runner
highlight: Twice a day along the wide Missouri: Hermann’s German wine town, the capitol at Jefferson City and ragtime Sedalia between the two big cities.

name: VIA Jonquière
highlight: A flag-stop wilderness train: nine hours through Laurentides lake country few roads reach, to the Saguenay fjord railhead of Jonquière.

name: Railjet Wien–Lienz
highlight: Osttirol’s capital link restored: two railjets a day over the Semmering, through the new Koralm tunnel and up the Drau valley. A child of the Dec 2025 timetable.

name: Jižní expres
highlight: Czechia’s first 200 km/h running: the rebuilt Fourth Corridor past Tábor’s Hussite hilltop to the Budweiser city, a record 85 minutes on the fastest Pendolinos.

name: München–Innsbruck
highlight: The Brenner corridor’s northern approach: out of Munich, across the Inn at Rosenheim, into Tyrol at Kufstein and up the valley beneath the Karwendel wall.

name: Railjet · Deutsches Eck
highlight: Tyrol to Salzburg the fast way, through Bavaria: Austrian expresses cut the German corner nonstop via Rosenheim, Alps on the horizon the whole run.

name: EC Transalpin
highlight: One train, one panorama car, half the Alps: Zurich to Graz over the Arlberg, past Zell am See, the Ennstal and the Gesäuse gates. The day-long EuroCity people ride for the window.

name: IC Hamburg–Köln
highlight: Germany’s busiest conventional corridor: ports to Ruhr through Bremen, Münster and five more big cities. Twice an hour, and no high-speed line in sight.

name: IC 1
highlight: Switzerland’s flagship express and spine of the clockface timetable: Zurich to Geneva across the Mittelland, Bern and Lausanne on the way, every half hour.

name: REX Wien–Bratislava
highlight: Europe’s closest capital pair, an hour apart on the 1848 Marchegg line across the Morava floodplain: two countries, one commuter corridor.

name: EuroCity Hungaria corridor
highlight: The Danube-bend main line: EuroCities every two hours sweeping past Štúrovo and the great river’s knee at Visegrád into Budapest.

name: alex München–Praha
highlight: The only direct Munich–Prague train: a famously unhurried crossing of the Bavarian Forest and Bohemia while the corridor awaits its wires.

name: EuroNight Praha–Zürich
highlight: The Czech–Swiss night link revived in 2023: the Elbe sandstone gorge at dusk, the Rhine plain at dawn, Zurich by breakfast.

name: EuroCity Budapest–Zagreb
highlight: The only Hungary–Croatia day train: along Balaton’s southern shore, over the Drava at Gyékényes and down through Zagorje to Zagreb.

name: EC Hornád
highlight: Budapest’s only direct reach into eastern Slovakia: the little EuroCity that grows at Miskolc, bound for Košice’s Gothic cathedral square.

name: IC Kraków–Wrocław
highlight: Poland’s two great tourist cities linked across industrial Silesia on the 1847 Upper Silesian Railway, the mesh line no Warsaw-bound train covers.

name: IC Budapest–Szeged
highlight: Hourly ICs across the Great Plain to Hungary’s paprika capital and its vast Votive Church. The southern spoke of the MÁV intercity star.

name: Wolsztyn Steam
highlight: Europe’s last everyday steam: commuters behind a 1948 Pt47 out of the working Wolsztyn roundhouse. An ordinary ticket, an extraordinary train.

name: IC 3
highlight: The approach every Glacier and Bernina rider actually takes: along Lake Zurich and the Walensee’s cliff wall to Chur, where the narrow gauge begins.

name: IC Poznań–Szczecin
highlight: Continuation of the Warsaw expresses to the Baltic’s big absent city: Szczecin’s Prussian boulevards and the gateway to Świnoujście.

name: Szeged–Békéscsaba railway
highlight: Line 135 strikes east across the Great Hungarian Plain through Hódmezővásárhely and Orosháza; the rails carry on past Békéscsaba to Salonta, over a border drawn in 1920.

name: Poznań–Piła railway
highlight: Built in 1879 to hook Poznań onto the Prussian Eastern Railway; a recent rebuild cut about fifteen minutes off the run north through Chodzież to Piła.

name: Main-Weser Railway
highlight: One of Germany’s first trunk railways, opened in stages between 1849 and 1852 through Gießen and Marburg; its 160 km/h ceiling is only reachable on the southern half.

name: Rome–Sulmona–Pescara railway
highlight: Rome to the Adriatic the hard way, over the Apennines by Tivoli, the drained Fucino basin at Avezzano and Sulmona, where the Transiberiana d’Italia branches into the Abruzzo highlands.

name: Ionian Railway
highlight: Six hours down the instep and toe of Italy, from Taranto by Metaponto, Sibari and Crotone to the Strait of Messina; the sections were joined into one railway in 1875.

name: Zafra–Huelva railway
highlight: Built in 1889 to carry Sierra de Aracena ore down to the quays at Huelva, and still crossing it past halts named for villages miles from the line: Jabugo, Almonaster, Valdelamusa.

name: Stångådalsbanan
highlight: Four separate railways stitched into one 235 kilometre run across Småland; the last section opened in 1902, and only since 1996 has the trip been possible without changing trains.

name: Poitiers–La Rochelle railway
highlight: The Paris TGVs peel off at Poitiers and finish on this line, opened to Niort in 1856 and to La Rochelle the year after: ninety minutes across the Poitou plain to the Atlantic.

name: Bordeaux–Hendaye railway
highlight: Dead straight down the Landes pine forest to the Basque coast; the rails left Bordeaux in 1841 and took until 1864 to reach the Spanish border at Irun.

name: Amiens–Rouen railway
highlight: Opened complete on 18 April 1867 rather than in stages, and still the cross country way from Picardy into Normandy by Poix-de-Picardie, Abancourt and Serqueux.

name: Halle–Halberstadt railway
highlight: The Halle end of the line that reached Vienenburg in 1872, ninety two kilometres by Könnern, Sandersleben and Aschersleben to Halberstadt on the northern edge of the Harz.

name: Lower Left Rhine Railway
highlight: The Rhine’s quiet left bank to the Dutch border: Kempen, Geldern, the pilgrim town of Kevelaer and Goch, on rails that reached Kleve on 1 March 1863.

name: Manresa–Lleida railway
highlight: Inland Catalonia the slow way, over the Segarra plateau by Calaf and Cervera; the first trains ran into Lleida in 1860 while the coastal route through Valls took the traffic.

name: Turin–Genoa railway
highlight: Five years of tunnelling under the Apennines opened this line in December 1853, and the 3.3 km Giovi tunnel at its summit was then the longest in the world.

name: Domodossola–Milan railway
highlight: The Simplon’s Italian approach, down the Toce and along the western shore of Lake Maggiore by Stresa and Arona; the rails reached Domodossola in 1888.

name: Verona–Bologna railway
highlight: Thirty seven years to cross the Po plain: begun at Bologna in 1887, over the river at Ostiglia in 1911 and finished into Verona on 1 February 1924. Fifty two minutes now.

name: Milan–Bologna classic line
highlight: The old road through Emilia by Lodi, Piacenza, Parma, Reggio and Modena, single track when it opened in 1861 and doubled by 1894; the Frecce take the high speed line beside it.

name: Dresden–Görlitz railway
highlight: Saxony end to end through Bautzen and the Lusatian hills, opened in stages from November 1845 and formally complete on 1 September 1847.

name: Vendsyssel Line
highlight: The last railway in Jutland, through Brønderslev and Hjørring to the ferry quays at Frederikshavn; it reached Aalborg itself in 1879, when the Limfjord bridge opened.

name: Zalaegerszeg–Boba railway
highlight: Up the Zala valley on rails the Transdanubian local company laid: Boba to Ukk in January 1889, on through Zalaegerszeg in October 1890, and now the first leg of the line to Slovenia.

name: Udine–Trieste railway
highlight: Friuli to the Adriatic through Gorizia and out along the Carso above Miramare; the last two sections opened three days apart in October 1860.

name: Prato–Bologna Direttissima
highlight: The 1934 Direttissima under the Apennines: an 18.5 km base tunnel, then the second longest in the world, and 180 km/h where the old line over the pass managed 75.

name: Ljubljana–Jesenice railway
highlight: The Slovenian half of the Rudolf Railway, opened complete on 14 December 1870, up the Sava by Škofja Loka and Kranj to the mouth of the Karawanks tunnel.

name: Gotha–Leinefelde railway
highlight: Forty two minutes across the Thuringian Basin through Bad Langensalza and Mühlhausen, opened in 1870 and now rebuilt for 160 km/h.

name: Northwest Line
highlight: Zealand from Roskilde out to the Great Belt at Kalundborg, opened on 30 December 1874 and doubled as far as Holbæk in 2014.

name: Oldenburg–Osnabrück railway
highlight: Across the Oldenburg moors and the Artland by Cloppenburg and Quakenbrück; opened as far as Quakenbrück in October 1875 and through to Osnabrück on 15 November 1876.

name: Saalbahn
highlight: Forty two minutes up the Saale gorge from Jena by Kahla, Orlamünde and Rudolstadt, on a line opened through to Saalfeld on 30 April 1874.

name: Plovdiv–Karlovo railway
highlight: North out of Plovdiv to the Rose Valley at Karlovo under the Balkan range, sixty one kilometres opened on 28 September 1933.

name: Kinnekullebanan
highlight: Four small railways stitched round the flat-topped hill of Kinnekulle by Lidköping and Mariestad, the last piece laid in 1910 and the whole of it regauged to standard by 1953.

name: Lahn Valley Railway
highlight: The Lahn from Wetzlar down to the Rhine through Weilburg, Limburg, Nassau and the spa at Bad Ems; opened in three pieces and finished on 10 January 1863.

name: Civitanova Marche–Fabriano railway
highlight: Off the Adriatic at Civitanova and up the Chienti and Potenza valleys by Macerata and Matelica; begun in 1884 at the far end and joined up in 1888.

name: Lemvigbanen
highlight: A Danish local line that never belonged to the state: Vemb to the fishing port of Thyborøn by Lemvig and Harboøre, finished on 1 November 1899 and still privately run.

name: Hohenlohebahn
highlight: Up the Kocher from Heilbronn through Schwäbisch Hall to Crailsheim; the first half opened in August 1862 and the rest waited until 10 December 1867.

name: Frankenwaldbahn
highlight: The climb over the Frankenwald from the Main valley to the Thuringian border at Probstzella by Kronach and Ludwigsstadt, finished in October 1885 and steep enough to need banking engines.

name: Delmenhorst–Hesepe railway
highlight: The Oldenburg south line through Vechta and Lohne, built in four pieces between 1888 and 1 May 1900, and still eighty kilometres an hour the whole way.

name: Avezzano–Roccasecca railway
highlight: Up the Liri from Roccasecca by Arce, Sora and Balsorano into the Fucino basin; eighteen years from the first section in 1884 to the last on 20 August 1902.

name: Mátészalka–Záhony railway
highlight: Opened on 27 September 1905 as a local line from Nagykároly to Csap; the border of 1920 cut it in three, and this is the Hungarian piece, out to the frontier at Záhony.

name: Binsui Line
highlight: The eastern arm of the old Chinese Eastern Railway, running provisionally from November 1901 and opened properly on 14 July 1903; ten hours from Harbin to the Russian border at Suifenhe.

name: Jōban Line
highlight: Tokyo to Sendai up the Pacific coast, inland of the Shinkansen: complete on 1 April 1905, and reopened right through Fukushima in March 2020 after nine years shut.

name: Golești–Câmpulung railway
highlight: Inaugurated on 21 June 1887 and derailed two months later between Mihăești and Stâlpeni; still an hour and a half up the Râul Târgului to Câmpulung.

name: Hatvan–Újszász railway
highlight: Down the Zagyva through the Jaszsag, opened on 10 March 1873 with four stations on it and electrified a century later in 1975.

name: TGV Paris–Luxembourg
highlight: The only direct rail link between the two capitals: 320 km/h across Champagne on the LGV Est, then down the Moselle past Metz’s golden cathedral.

name: Nomad Krono+
highlight: Normandy’s trunk from Saint-Lazare: Lisieux, Caen and Bayeux of the Tapestry, out along the Cotentin to the great naval harbour of Cherbourg.

name: Nomad Krono
highlight: The Impressionists’ line down the Seine: Vernon for Giverny, Rouen’s spires, and the ferro-concrete UNESCO city at the river’s mouth.

name: European Sleeper
highlight: The night train that replaced the lost Nightjet: Paris to Berlin via Brussels three times a week since March 2026, the open-access sleeper’s boldest route yet.

name: Intercités
highlight: The Atlantic link that skips Paris: marshes of the Vendée, La Rochelle’s towers and the Charente to Bordeaux. Ridership has doubled, and it is contracted to 2036.

name: Intercités
highlight: France’s great west–east diagonal, no Paris required: the Loire at Angers and Tours, Bourges’ cathedral, then Roanne and the Lyon hills.

name: Alvia
highlight: Gauge-changing Alvias to the Basque coast: the 2022 Burgos high-speed line, Vitoria’s green ring and the belle-époque bay of La Concha at the end.

name: Alvia
highlight: Off the high-speed line at Palencia and over the 1866 Reinosa pass, then a mountain descent to the Cantabrian Sea and Santander’s curved bay.

name: Avant Eje Atlántico
highlight: Galicia’s rebuilt Atlantic spine: 250 km/h between the rías with Santiago de Compostela halfway. The north–south line Madrid’s radial map forgets.

name: TGV Rhin-Rhône
highlight: France’s only province-to-province LGV: Burgundy to Alsace without a glance at Paris, Dijon and Belfort on the way to the cathedral city.

name: TGV Paris–Brest
highlight: To Brittany’s Atlantic tip: the 2017 LGV to Rennes, then the granite north coast by Saint-Brieuc and Morlaix’s viaduct to the naval roadstead of Brest.

name: TGV Paris–Quimper
highlight: Brittany’s other arm: the same 2017 high speed line to Rennes, where the Brest and Quimper halves of the train part company, then south to the Morbihan coast by Vannes, Auray and Lorient to Quimper in Finistère.

name: Intercités de Nuit
highlight: The Pyrenean pilgrim night train: out of Austerlitz every evening on the classic line through Poitiers and Dax, waking beneath the mountains at Lourdes.

name: Intercity Tirreno
highlight: The Tyrrhenian artery the high-speed network bypasses: Maremma’s coast, Pisa, the marble Apuans and the whole Riviera di Levante into Genoa.

name: Milano–Tirano
highlight: Lake Como’s eastern shore from the train window: Varenna, then the vineyard terraces of the Valtellina to Tirano, where the Bernina Express waits.

name: Bari–Matera
highlight: The only railway to the Sassi: a 950 mm oddity climbing the Murgia plateau from Bari to cave-city Matera, every visitor’s first sight of Basilicata.

name: Avant Madrid–Toledo
highlight: Thirty-three minutes off the Seville high-speed line to the city on the Tagus bend: El Greco’s Toledo as a Madrid day trip.

name: Mr Henderson’s Railway
highlight: Up the Serranía de Ronda from Gibraltar bay: the British-built 1892 line that is Mr Henderson’s railway proper, Algeciras to the Bobadilla plain, ending today at Antequera Santa Ana’s high-speed interchange.

name: Rodalies R3
highlight: Climbs from Barcelona to 1,494 m at Toses, the roof of the Spanish network, to meet the Yellow Train across the platform at Latour-de-Carol.

name: Intercidades
highlight: Across the Tagus and into the cork-oak Alentejo: ninety minutes from Lisbon to Évora’s Roman temple and bone chapel.

name: Linha do Algarve
highlight: The Algarve coast end to end: Portimão, Silves’ red castle, Faro and the Ria Formosa lagoons out to Vila Real de Santo António on the Guadiana. Every summer visitor’s slow shuttle.

name: Thrace InterCity
highlight: Greece’s only train across Thrace: 440 km laid in 1896 for the Salonika–Constantinople railway, threading the Nestos gorge between Drama and Xanthi.

name: Pamukkale Ekspresi
highlight: Heir of the Haydarpaşa night express: 418 km across the Aegean interior via Kütahya, Afyon and Dinar, down to Denizli’s white travertine country.

name: Osoblažka
highlight: Czechia’s last public narrow gauge: 760 mm and 102 curves in 20 km (including the network’s sharpest, at 75 m radius), dawdling across Silesia at 40 km/h.

name: Żnin District Railway
highlight: A 600 mm minirailway from 1894 chuffing 12 km through Pałuki to the Iron Age lake fort of Biskupin, where archaeologists commute by narrow gauge.

name: Nadmorska Kolej Wąskotorowa
highlight: Opened 1896 and still packing 150,000 riders a summer: metre-gauge cars amble from Gryfice to the Baltic cliffs, Poland’s last coastal narrow gauge.

name: Upper Silesian Narrow Gauge
highlight: Running since 1853, the world’s oldest continuously operating narrow gauge: 785 mm industrial track turned heritage line across the Silesian coalfield.

name: Mocănița Huțulca
highlight: Bucovina’s oldest mocănița, laid in 1888 for a Munich sawmill: the Huțulca puffs 12 km up the Moldovița valley behind a Reșița-built 764 steam engine.

name: Mocănița Sovata
highlight: From the spa resort of Sovata a 1949 Chrzanów steam engine hauls open cars to Câmpu Cetății, on a rescued shard of the 82 km Târgu Mureș–Praid line of 1915.

name: Katakolo–Olympia Train
highlight: Greece’s first provincial railway (1882–83) reborn as a cruise shuttle: a metre-gauge railcar links Katakolo’s quay with the sanctuary of Ancient Olympia.

name: Orava Forest Railway
highlight: Built by POWs in 1915–18 to haul timber: the surviving 3.5 km climbs from Tanečník to Sedlo Beskyd on a five-switchback staircase unique in Europe.

name: Posázavský Pacifik
highlight: Prague’s “Pacific”, the tramps’ weekend railway of the 1920s: ledges above the Vltava and Sázava canyons and the 41 m Žampach viaduct on the way to Čerčany.

name: 6 Eylül Ekspresi
highlight: Heir of the Bandırma boat trains that sped İzmir–Istanbul travellers to the Marmara ferries: relaunched in 2023, 341 km via Manisa and Balıkesir.

name: Northern Trans-Iranian
highlight: The Trans-Iranian’s UNESCO-listed northern arm: night sleepers spiral down the Alborz over the Veresk bridge, from Tehran’s desert rim to the Caspian plain.

name: Weißeritztalbahn
highlight: Germany’s oldest working public narrow gauge (1882): 750 mm steam daily through the Rabenauer Grund gorge and past Malter dam, 350 m up into the Ore Mountains to Kipsdorf.

name: Lößnitzgrundbahn
highlight: Daily steam on Dresden’s doorstep since 1884: out of Radebeul’s villa streets into the wooded Lößnitzgrund, past Moritzburg’s moated hunting palace to little Radeburg.

name: Harzquerbahn
highlight: HSB’s metre-gauge trunk across the Harz: 2-10-2 tank engines storm out of Nordhausen up the Zorge valley to Drei Annen Hohne, the junction where the Brocken steam begins.

name: Berner Oberland-Bahn
highlight: Jungfrau gateway since 1890: from Interlaken Ost the BOB splits at Zweilütschinen. One arm goes to Lauterbrunnen; this one climbs to Grindelwald under the Eiger’s north face.

name: Waldviertelbahn
highlight: NÖVOG’s 760 mm Südast winds from Gmünd through the granite-and-pine Waldviertel to Groß Gerungs, summer steam grinding round horseshoe bends and over stone viaducts.

name: Murtalbahn
highlight: Austria’s second-longest narrow gauge (1894) follows the young Mur 64 km from Unzmarkt to Tamsweg: 70 km/h diesels on weekdays, steam specials all summer.

name: Chemins de fer du Jura
highlight: Metre gauge across the Franches-Montagnes plateau: horse pastures and firs at 1,000 m from watch-town La Chaux-de-Fonds to Saignelégier, then a wooded ravine descent to Glovelier.

name: Brohltalbahn
highlight: The Vulkan-Expreß ambles at Tempo 20 from the Rhine at Brohl 400 m up into the volcanic Eifel, on metre gauge laid in 1901 to carry the region’s tuff and phonolite.

name: Drachenfelsbahn
highlight: Germany’s oldest rack railway (1883) climbs 220 m in eight minutes from Königswinter past Schloss Drachenburg to the Drachenfels ruin above the Rhine, Siegfried’s dragon mountain.

name: Borkumer Kleinbahn
highlight: Timed to the tide: Borkum’s 900 mm railway (1888) meets every ferry at the Reede pier and rolls 7 km along the dike into the North Sea island’s town.

name: Reblaus-Express
highlight: Named after the phylloxera louse: a heritage diesel with a wine-tavern car trundles from Retz’s vine terraces to the Thaya loop at Drosendorf, weekends May to October.

name: Blonay–Chamby Museum Railway
highlight: Switzerland’s first museum railway (running since 1968): Belle Époque steam and electrics cross the Baye de Clarens viaduct high above Lake Geneva on 3 km of 1902 branch line.

name: Preßnitztalbahn
highlight: Torn up in 1986, relaid 1992–2000 by volunteers: Saxon IV K tanks once more steam the upper Preßnitz valley from Steinbach to Jöhstadt on weekends through the year.

name: Steyrtal-Museumsbahn
highlight: Austria’s oldest 760 mm line (1889): ÖGEG steam ambles down the green Steyr valley from Steyr Lokalbahnhof to Grünburg on summer weekends. Bosnian gauge as it began.

name: Wangerooger Inselbahn
highlight: Deutsche Bahn’s only narrow gauge: the tide writes the timetable as diesels haul ferry passengers across the salt marsh from Westanleger pier to car-free Wangerooge village.

name: KTM ETS3
highlight: Electric at last to the peninsula’s tip: since December 2025 the ETS3 EMUs run Kuala Lumpur–Johor Bahru direct, ending a nine-year rail gap to Malaysia’s second city.

name: Mutiara Timur
highlight: Java’s eastern express since 1973, tracing the north coast past Probolinggo before winding through coffee country to the Bali ferry pier at Ketapang.

name: Rajabasa
highlight: South Sumatra’s all-day economy flagship: nine and a half hours and dozens of halts through rubber, coal and pepper country from Palembang to Bandar Lampung.

name: Sribilah Utama
highlight: North Sumatra’s mainline stalwart since 1978, rolling out of Medan across plantation flatlands to the railhead town of Rantau Prapat.

name: Hotan–Ruoqiang Railway
highlight: The 2022 desert line that closed the world’s first rail loop around a sand sea: 825 km along the Taklamakan’s southern rim on viaducts built to let the dunes blow through.

name: Chuanqing Railway
highlight: China’s mountain railway to fairyland: 200 km/h from the Chengdu plain up the Min valley to Huangshengguan, the new gateway station for Jiuzhaigou and Huanglong.

name: Harbin–Mohe Snow Country Train
highlight: The “Snow Country Train” heads 17 hours north to China’s northernmost station at Mohe, where −40 °C winters, frost forests and the odd aurora reward the ride.

name: Binzhou Railway
highlight: The Chinese Eastern Railway’s west arm, working since 1902: over the Greater Khingan to the Russian border at Manzhouli, where the Trans-Manchurian crosses to Zabaikalsk.

name: Jingha Railway
highlight: Its Tangshan–Tianjin end opened in 1881 as the Kaiping Tramway and is the oldest railway still working in China; the Z15 runs the whole 1,249 km overnight in ten hours.

name: S-train (Namdo Ocean)
highlight: Since September 2025 the S-train sweeps the whole south coast from Busan to Mokpo, crossing the brand-new Boseong–Imseongri line past tea fields and tidal bays.

name: Isan Watthana
highlight: Thailand’s smartest sleeper: Chinese-built berths glide out of Bangkok at dusk and wake along the Mun River in Ubon Ratchathani, deep in southern Isan.

name: Sabah State Railway
highlight: Borneo’s only railway, opened to Tenom in 1905: a metre-gauge survivor that squeezes through the roaring Padas Gorge on its jungle climb inland.

name: Gajayana
train: KAI New Generation executive & luxury coaches
highlight: KAI’s flagship sleeper since 1999 leaves Jakarta after dark and skirts Java’s southern volcanoes to reach highland Malang in time for breakfast.

name: A-train (Jeongseon Arirang)
highlight: The Arirang-themed A-train leaves the Jungang main line at Jecheon and threads the Jeongseon canyon to Auraji, where two mountain torrents meet.

name: Rail Cruise Haerang
highlight: Korea’s only sleeper cruise: three days around the entire peninsula from Seoul (Suncheon Bay, Busan, Gyeongju, the Jeongdongjin sunrise), with the train as the hotel.

name: G-train (West Gold)
highlight: The West Gold train ambles down the Janghang line’s tidal-flat coast, foot baths steaming on board, with Daecheon beach and the Geum estuary out the window.

name: Dunhuang Sleeper Y667/668
highlight: The branded “Dunhuang” sleeper leaves Lanzhou at 18:00 and follows the Hexi Corridor’s Great Wall forts overnight, arriving near the Mogao caves by dawn.

name: Golmud–Korla Railway
highlight: Opened 2020 across the Altun Shan between Qinghai and Xinjiang: 1,206 km of salt flats, desert and near-total emptiness. One of the loneliest overnight rides on Earth.

name: Petit train d’Artouste
highlight: Built for the dam works of the 1920s: 500 mm open cars creep along a cliff ledge at 1,940 m from the La Sagette gondola to Lac d’Artouste.

name: Train à Vapeur des Cévennes
highlight: Steam between Anduze and Saint-Jean-du-Gard: across the Gardon on four viaducts, past the giant bamboo of Prafrance. Forty open-window minutes in the Cévennes.

name: Oran–Béchar Night Train
highlight: Algeria’s Sahara sleeper, revived in December 2024: couchettes leave Oran at nightfall and reach Béchar at the Saoura’s edge by sunrise.

name: Le Train Rouge
highlight: France’s longest tourist railway: 60 km from Rivesaltes’ vineyards into the Fenouillèdes gorges beneath the Cathar castles of Quéribus and Puilaurens.

name: Intercités de Nuit
highlight: Asleep out of Austerlitz, awake on the Côte Vermeille: the sleeper threads Collioure, Port-Vendres and Banyuls to the last stop before Spain.

name: Ligne de la Côte Bleue
highlight: An everyday TER on a corniche of 23 tunnels and 18 viaducts: calanque after calanque between L’Estaque and Martigues for a few euros.

name: Panoramique des Dômes
highlight: A Strub rack railway spirals up the dormant Puy de Dôme volcano: 5.3 km and 500 vertical metres to the Roman Temple of Mercury at 1,406 m.

name: Le Grand Tour
highlight: Puy du Fou’s rolling theatre: a Belle Époque sleeper loops 4,000 km around France in six days, actors staging a mystery from Reims to Chenonceau.

name: Intercités de Nuit
highlight: The Aveyron sleeper: off the Limoges main line at Brive, then Rocamadour, the Lot valley and Rodez by breakfast, with Albi through-cars on weekends.

name: Velay Express
highlight: France’s highest steam railway: a 1906 Mallet hauls metre-gauge trains across the 1,000 m Velay plateau between Raucoules and Saint-Agrève.

name: Chemin de fer de la Vendée
operator: Chemin de Fer de la Vendée
highlight: Belle-Époque dining on the move: restored CIWL Orient Express diners behind an 030 T steam engine, three viaducts between Mortagne and Les Herbiers.

name: Train des Mouettes
highlight: Steam at 30 km/h beside the Seudre oyster beds: an 1891 Schneider, France’s oldest working steam engine, still hauls the gulls’ train to La Tremblade.

name: Train Thur Doller Alsace
highlight: Sunday steam in the Doller valley: a century-old 030 T ambles from Cernay to Sentheim past storks, orchards and the first folds of the Vosges.

name: Dia Tsara
highlight: Madagascar’s east-coast revival of 2023: once a week, twelve hours from Moramanga through rainforest gorges to the Pangalanes shore and Toamasina.

name: Tren Solar de la Quebrada
operator: Tren Solar de la Quebrada S.E.
highlight: Lithium-battery railcars charged by a solar farm glide through the UNESCO-listed Quebrada de Humahuaca to Tilcara: the first solar-powered train in the Americas.

name: Media Distancia R-3f
highlight: Three metre-gauge trains a day still thread all 119 km of the 1898 Santander–Bilbao railway, winding through green Basque and Cantabrian valleys.

name: Ferrocarril de Riotinto
train: Restored mine coaches; steam on winter Sundays
highlight: Restored mining stock creeps along the blood-red Río Tinto through a Mars-like landscape mined for 5,000 years, and Victorian steam hauls it on winter Sundays.

name: Maria Fumaça (VFCJ)
highlight: Brazil’s flagship steam railway: ABPF volunteers fire century-old locomotives up the 1875 Mogiana trunk from Campinas to Jaguariúna every weekend.

name: Caminho de Ferro de Moçâmedes
train: CFM weekly express, restaurant & multimedia cars
highlight: Angola’s third great trunk climbs from the desert port of Namibe over the Serra da Chela to Menongue: 756 rebuilt km, with a weekly express since December 2023.

name: Tren Macho
highlight: Peru’s beloved Tren Macho is back: free trains roll the first 57 km down the Mantaro valley to Cuenca while the century-old Huancavelica line is modernized.

name: Bonde de Santa Teresa
highlight: Latin America’s oldest electric tramway (1896) rattles across the Carioca Aqueduct’s arches and up Santa Teresa’s cobbled lanes high above downtown Rio.

name: Tren de Felipe II
highlight: An ALCO diesel and 1940s coaches staffed by costumed actors climb from Príncipe Pío into the Guadarrama foothills to Philip II’s colossal monastery-palace.

name: Expresso Turístico
highlight: A 1952 ALCO diesel and 1960s Budd cars leave Luz station on weekends for Paranapiacaba, the fog-wrapped English railway village at the rim of the Serra do Mar.

name: Media Distancia R-1f
highlight: Europe’s longest narrow-gauge ride: two trains a day take seven hours to weave around Galicia’s rias and along the Asturian cliffs from Ferrol to Oviedo.

name: Treno Natura
highlight: Steam excursions across the UNESCO Val d’Orcia: 51 km of cypress avenues, clay badlands and Brunello vineyards on an 1865 branch kept alive purely for the Treno Natura.

name: Porrettana Express
highlight: The 1864 Porrettana was Italy’s first railway across the Apennines: E.626-hauled Centoporte coaches now relive its 26 ‰ climb from Pistoia to the spa town of Porretta.

name: Trenino Verde
highlight: The Trenino Verde’s second living branch: 46 km of 950 mm track twisting off Macomer’s basalt plateau down to the palm-lined seafront at Bosa Marina.

name: Irpinia Express
highlight: Closed in 2010, revived for excursions: the 1895 Ofanto-valley line threads 119 km of viaducts, vineyards and hill villages from Avellino to lonely Rocchetta junction.

name: Treno di Dante
operator: Il Treno di Dante · Fondazione FS
highlight: Vintage Centoporte coaches link Dante’s Florence with his tomb in Ravenna over the Apennine Faentina line, joined by new direct Sunday trains since July 2026.

name: Ferrovia Trento–Malè–Mezzana
highlight: A metre-gauge electric line out of Trento: through the Rocchetta gorge into apple-carpeted Val di Non and Val di Sole, ending at Mezzana beneath the Brenta Dolomites.

name: Chemin de Fer à Vapeur des Trois Vallées
highlight: Steam on the 1854 Entre-Sambre-et-Meuse line: CFV3V engines bark up the wooded Viroin valley to the great museum shed at Treignes.

name: Lennakatten
highlight: Steam from the edge of a university city: the 891 mm Lennakatten rolls 33 km through Uppland forests and lakeside summer halts to the engine sheds at Faringe.

name: Krøderbanen
highlight: Norway’s longest museum railway: 26 km of the 1872 Krøder line preserved whole, with stations, water cranes and NSB steam between Vikersund and the lake at Krøderen.

name: Gamle Vossebanen
highlight: The 1883 Voss line’s surviving loop outside Bergen: NSB 18c steam between Garnes and Midttun, bypassed by new tunnels in 1964 and kept alive by volunteers.

name: Thamshavnbanen
highlight: Built in 1908 for Orkla’s copper ore: the oldest alternating-current railway still in service, running its original 6.6 kV motor coaches along the green Orkla valley.

name: Setesdalsbanen
highlight: Norway’s oldest museum railway, volunteer-run since 1964: 1890s narrow-gauge steam puffing up the Otra river from Grovane to the little terminus at Røyknes.

name: Veluwsche Stoomtrein
highlight: The Netherlands’ biggest steam operation: wartime German Kriegsloks and a forty-strong fleet work the 1887 Veluwe country line between Apeldoorn and Dieren.

name: Mariager–Handest Veteranjernbane
highlight: Denmark’s leading veteran railway: 1909 Henschel steam from the fjord port of Mariager over rolling moraine hills to Handest, run in 1950s private-railway style.

name: TOHOKU EMOTION
highlight: A restaurant on rails (open kitchen car, chef’s courses at every seat) rolling the Sanriku surf from Hachinohe to Kuji along the Tanesashi coast.

name: Tama Densha
highlight: Eiji Mitooka’s white train painted with 101 cartoon Tamas trundles to Kishi, where calico stationmaster Tama famously saved the line; a cat shrine now guards the platform.

name: SL Banetsu Monogatari
highlight: C57 180, “the Lady”, hauls seven retro coaches up the Agano river gorge from Niitsu to castle-town Aizu-Wakamatsu, one of Japan’s last full-size mainline steam runs.

name: Setsugekka
highlight: Crimson-and-silver resort train with Japan’s largest train windows, serving regional courses on a slow sweep from Mt Myoko’s snow country to the Sea of Japan at Itoigawa.

name: Iyonada Monogatari
highlight: A retro maroon-and-gold diner idling along the Iyonada shore: brunch above the waves and a pause at Shimonada, Japan’s most photographed seaside platform.

name: Kairi
highlight: Kairi means “sea and village”: a hybrid diner serving Niigata and Shonai delicacies while threading the Sasagawa-nagare, 11 km of wave-gnawed rocks on the Uetsu coast.

name: GRAN Tenku
highlight: Nankai’s deep-red 2026 flagship runs through from Namba’s neon to Gokurakubashi, grinding up 50‰ cedar slopes to the cable car for sacred Koyasan, with a lounge and bar aboard.

name: Umisachi-Yamasachi
highlight: Obi-cedar railcars named for the sea-luck, mountain-luck myth skim the Nichinan palm coast past Aoshima’s Devil’s Washboard reefs to the fishing port of Nango.

name: A-Train (Amakusa)
highlight: A jazz-soundtracked bar on rails (dark wood, stained glass, “A-Highball” in hand) swinging along the Ariake tidal flats from Kumamoto to the Amakusa ferry at Misumi.

name: HIGH RAIL 1375
highlight: Grinds to 1,375 m at JR’s highest rail point below Yatsugatake: observatory seats by day, a stargazing dome and astronomer-guided night runs under the Milky Way.

name: etSETOra
highlight: etSETOra drifts the Kure Line’s island-studded Seto shore with Hiroshima patissiers’ sweets courses and a sake bar. Since 2025 it runs clear through to Fukuyama.

name: SL Paleo Express
highlight: The closest steam to Tokyo: wartime C58 363 huffs four retro coaches from Kumagaya into the Chichibu hills past Nagatoro’s rock terraces, running since 1988.

name: Koshino Shu*Kura
highlight: A sake brewery on wheels (Niigata tasting bar, live jazz, a long pause on the sea cliff at Aoumigawa) winding via Nagaoka into snow-country Tokamachi.

name: Belles montagnes et mer
highlight: “Beautiful mountains and sea”: an emerald art-gallery railcar where a sushi chef works the counter as Amaharashi bay frames 3,000-metre Tateyama across the water.

name: Blue Symphony
highlight: Navy-and-gold Blue Symphony glides from Osaka Abenobashi to holy Yoshino, the UNESCO cherry mountain, with a lounge bar, cake sets and armchairs in a reborn commuter train.

name: Tosa Toki no Yoake no Monogatari
highlight: Ryoma-themed “dawn of a new era” train pairs Tosa seafood with Pacific panoramas above Susaki and Tosa-Kure bays, locals waving it through tea fields to Kubokawa.

name: Hanayome Noren
highlight: A rolling Kaga bridal curtain: vermilion-and-black cars finished in Wajima-lacquer motifs and gold leaf, serving Ishikawa sweets en route to Wakura Onsen’s seaside baths.

name: Rokumon
highlight: Rokumon wears the Sanada clan’s six-coin crest in deep crimson, serving kaiseki under Mt Asama on the old Shinetsu main line from Karuizawa down to Zenko-ji’s Nagano.

name: Ametsuchi
highlight: Lapis-blue Ametsuchi (“heaven and earth”, from the Kojiki’s opening line) roams the San’in coast’s breakers past Mt Daisen and Lake Shinji from Tottori to Izumo.

name: Ruskeala Express
highlight: Russia’s only daily steam service: blue retro cars behind a vintage locomotive from Sortavala to Ruskeala’s flooded marble canyon, staged down to conductors in 1900s dress.

name: Night Express
highlight: Ukraine’s overnight hop across the Carpathians: asleep through Lviv, awake for the climb past Skole into the 2018 twin-bore Beskyd tunnel, then down the valley to Uzhhorod.

name: Hutsulshchyna
highlight: Ukraine’s flagship sleeper into Hutsul country: dusk in Kyiv, dawn above the Prut gorge at Yaremche, then Vorokhta’s stone viaduct and the Yablunytsia pass down to Rakhiv.

name: Labytnangi
highlight: Fifty-two hours north to the last station on the Gulag-built Dead Road: the Chum–Labytnangi branch opened in 1948 and stops on the Ob, across the water from Salekhard.

name: Vorkuta
highlight: Two nights up the Stalin-era Pechora mainline to Vorkuta, a coal city beyond the Arctic Circle that no all-year road reaches; train № 41 is its lifeline to Moscow.

name: Premium
highlight: The southern flagship since 1964 (first Ritsa, then Sochi, Premium since 2009): 1,761 km from Kazansky station to the subtropical Black Sea platforms of Adler in 23 hours.

name: Yantar
highlight: Running since 1964, the Yantar threads Moscow to Russia’s Baltic exclave via Minsk and Vilnius, the last corridor where Russian passenger trains still cross the EU.

name: Sakhalin Night Train
highlight: Russia’s island sleeper: 613 km up Sakhalin’s east coast to oil-town Nogliki, on a railway begun under Japanese rule that kept its narrow gauge until regauging in 2019.

name: AYaM Yakutia Train
highlight: 23 hours north from the BAM at Tynda across permafrost to Nizhny Bestyakh on the Lena, one river crossing short of Yakutsk. Russia’s newest long-distance railway.

name: Zhemchuzhina Kavkaza
highlight: A hotel on rails looping from Moscow around the North Caucasus (Maykop, Kislovodsk, Vladikavkaz, Grozny, seaside Derbent and Nalchik): seven days, one ticket, since 2021.

name: Stoosbahn
highlight: The world’s steepest funicular: a 110% maximum gradient climbed by barrel cabins that rotate to keep the floor level, 744 m up to car-free Stoos.

name: Niesenbahn
train: Two-section funicular; car change at Schwandegg
highlight: Climbs 1,643 m over 3.5 km up the pyramid of the Niesen, and the service stairway alongside is the longest on earth at 11,674 steps.

name: Gelmerbahn
train: Open-air 24-seat cars of 1926, public rides since 2001
highlight: An open-car ride up a 106% grade, Europe’s steepest funicular until Stoos overtook it in 2017, built to serve the Gelmersee dam works.

name: Funiculaire Sierre–Crans-Montana
train: Fully renewed cars, track and drive (2022)
highlight: Switzerland’s longest funicular: 4.2 km and 927 m of climb from the Rhône valley vineyards at Sierre to the Crans-Montana plateau.

name: Fribourg Funicular
train: 1899 cars hauled by 3,000-litre wastewater ballast tanks
highlight: Europe’s last funicular driven by wastewater: since 1899 the descending car is weighted with up to 3,000 litres of city sewage.

name: Hungerburgbahn
train: Tilting-floor hybrid funicular cabins; Zaha Hadid stations
highlight: A 2007 hybrid funicular with Zaha Hadid’s sculpted glass stations. Its cabins tilt to stay level from the flat river crossing to a 46% climb.

name: FestungsBahn Salzburg
train: Panoramic glass cars from the 2011 renewal
highlight: Austria’s oldest funicular in service (1892) rises into Hohensalzburg, one of Europe’s largest intact medieval fortresses, in 54 seconds.

name: Mendelbahn
train: Two counterbalanced cars with passing loop
highlight: Europe’s longest and steepest funicular at its 1903 opening, still climbing 854 m at up to 64% from South Tyrol’s wine country to the Mendel Pass.

name: Como–Brunate Funicular
train: Two counterbalanced cars with mid-line passing loop
highlight: Since 1894 the link between Como’s lakefront and hilltop Brunate, ’the balcony of the Alps’, climbing at up to 55% above Lake Como.

name: Funicolare Centrale
train: Two four-car trains, about 450 passengers each
highlight: One of the world’s busiest funiculars: around 10 million passengers a year between Via Toledo and the Vomero hill.

name: Capri Funicular
train: Two counterbalanced trains between port and Piazzetta
highlight: Capri’s main street since 1907: hoists ferry arrivals from Marina Grande harbour 138 m up to the island’s famous Piazzetta in four minutes.

name: Montmartre Funicular
highlight: Paris’s shortcut to Sacré-Cœur since 1900: 108 m of track, 36 m of rise and about two million riders a year.

name: Fourvière Funicular (la ficelle)
highlight: Lyon ran the world’s first urban funiculars from 1862; today’s F2 of 1900 lifts riders from UNESCO-listed Vieux Lyon to the Fourvière basilica.

name: Tibidabo Funicular (Cuca de Llum)
train: Glass-roofed ’Cuca de Llum’ trains from the 2021 rebuild
highlight: Barcelona’s 1901 summit line to the Tibidabo amusement park and Sagrat Cor temple, reborn in 2021 as the glass ’glow-worm’ trains.

name: Montjuïc Funicular
train: Twin three-car trains from the 1992 Olympic rebuild
highlight: Metro-integrated since 1928 and rebuilt for the 1992 Olympics, and among Europe’s highest-capacity funiculars at 8,000 passengers an hour.

name: Bom Jesus do Monte Funicular
operator: Irmandade do Bom Jesus do Monte
highlight: The world’s oldest water-balance funicular in continuous service (1882), climbing beside the baroque stairway of UNESCO-listed Bom Jesus do Monte.

name: Budavári Sikló
train: Replica 19th-century wooden cars Margit and Gellért (1986)
highlight: Opened 1870 as Europe’s second funicular; destroyed in WWII and rebuilt in 1986, it climbs to Buda Castle inside the UNESCO Danube panorama.

name: Zagreb Funicular (Uspinjača)
highlight: At 66 m one of the world’s shortest public funiculars, linking Zagreb’s Lower and Upper Towns since 1890.

name: Ljubljana Castle Funicular
train: Single glass panoramic cabin with counterweight (2006)
highlight: A glass funicular of 2006 rising 70 m in one minute from the old-town market square to Ljubljana Castle, the capital’s defining landmark.

name: Fløibanen
highlight: Norway’s best-known funicular (1918): 844 m and ~300 m of rise from central Bergen to the Fløyen viewpoint above the fjord city.

name: Lynton & Lynmouth Cliff Railway
train: Original 1890 twin cars, each with a 700-gallon water tank
highlight: The world’s highest and steepest fully water-powered railway (1890): gravity and 700-gallon tanks alone work its twin cars on a 58% grade.

name: Nerobergbahn
train: Historic 1888 cars driven by 7,000-litre water ballast tanks
highlight: Germany’s only surviving water-ballast funicular (1888), still climbing Wiesbaden’s Neroberg on 7,000 litres of tank water and no engine.

name: Kyiv Funicular
highlight: Kyiv’s 1905 funicular climbs a 36% grade from riverside Podil to the St Michael’s monastery quarter, with 2.8 million riders a year even in wartime.

name: Tbilisi Funicular
train: Doppelmayr Garaventa cars from the 2012 reconstruction
highlight: Tbilisi’s 1905 funicular to Mtatsminda, the city’s highest viewpoint. Derelict after 2000, rebuilt by Doppelmayr Garaventa and reopened 2012.

name: Tünel
train: Two rubber-tyred cars from the 1971 electrification
highlight: Opened 1875: the world’s second-oldest underground urban railway after London’s, and the oldest underground funicular still running.

name: F1 Taksim–Kabataş Funicular
highlight: A deep-bored 2006 funicular linking Bosphorus ferries and trams at Kabataş with Taksim Square: Istanbul’s modern echo of the 1875 Tünel.

name: Monongahela Incline
highlight: Opened 1870, the oldest continuously operating funicular in the United States, and still a fare-integrated everyday transit link up Mount Washington.

name: Duquesne Incline
train: Original 1877 J.G. Brill wooden cars in cherry and oak
operator: Society for the Preservation of the Duquesne Heights Incline
highlight: Original 1877 wooden Brill cars still climb the 30-degree grade to Grandview Avenue and Pittsburgh’s postcard skyline overlook.

name: Lookout Mountain Incline Railway
train: Two counterbalanced cars with midway passing loop
highlight: ’America’s Most Amazing Mile’ since 1895: the 72.7% grade near the summit ranks among the steepest on any passenger railway.

name: Angels Flight
train: Twin 1901 cars Olivet and Sinai, restored 2017
highlight: Billed the world’s shortest incorporated railway since 1901, the 91 m Bunker Hill hop costs $1.50 and starred in film noir and La La Land.

name: Fenelon Place Elevator
train: Two counterbalanced house-shaped cars, winched at 41 degrees
highlight: Built in 1882 so banker J.K. Graves could ride the bluff home for lunch, and billed as the world’s shortest, steepest scenic railway.

name: Old Quebec Funicular
train: Two independent panoramic cabins from the 1998 rebuild
highlight: Scaling Cap Diamant at 45 degrees since 1879, it links Petit-Champlain’s boutiques to Dufferin Terrace beside the Château Frontenac.

name: Falls Incline Railway
train: Two enclosed 40-passenger cabins from the 2013 rebuild
highlight: Niagara Parks bills it the world’s slowest funicular: a 62-second, 3.5 km/h glide linking Fallsview’s hotels to Horseshoe Falls at Table Rock.

name: Funicular de Santiago
train: Two 1925 counterbalanced cars, rebuilt 2020–22, zoo mid-station
highlight: A 1925 funicular and national monument rising to Santiago’s hilltop Virgin. Pope John Paul II rode it during his 1987 visit.

name: Ascensor Concepción
train: Two seven-passenger cars at 46 degrees, once water-balance powered
highlight: Valparaíso’s oldest ascensor (1883) began on water ballast and still hoists riders 69 m from the Turri clock up to Paseo Gervasoni.

name: Monserrate Funicular
train: Two counterbalanced trains of up to 80 passengers
highlight: Hauling pilgrims since 1929 up 460 vertical metres to Bogotá’s 3,152 m summit sanctuary, one of the world’s highest funicular rides.

name: Plano Inclinado Gonçalves
train: Two 36-passenger cabins, re-equipped in the 2025 requalification
highlight: Built in 1874 with Esslingen machinery, Salvador’s cliff-face inclined plane still links the Comércio to UNESCO-listed Pelourinho, free of charge.

name: Flying Dutchman Funicular
train: Two 40-seat cars named after ships wrecked off the Cape
highlight: Africa’s only commercial funicular, named for the ghost ship said to haunt Cape Point, lifts visitors 87 m toward the 1859 lighthouse.

name: Peak Tram
highlight: Asia’s first funicular (1888), climbing almost 400 m over the Victoria Harbour skyline, with four million riders a year on 6th-generation cars.

name: Penang Hill Railway
highlight: Malaysia’s only funicular since 1923: the Swiss-rebuilt line climbs 691 m through what was once the steepest funicular tunnel in the world.

name: Carmelit
train: Two stepped Von Roll/Doppelmayr trains, refurbished 2018
highlight: Israel’s only fully underground railway and one of the world’s smallest metros: six stepped stations rising 274 m inside Mount Carmel.

name: Koyasan Cable Car
highlight: Nankai’s 1930 cable car hoists pilgrims up the final 328 m to UNESCO-listed Kōyasan, the mountaintop monastery town of Shingon Buddhism.

name: Hakone Tozan Cable Car
highlight: Japan’s second-oldest funicular (1921) links Gōra with the Hakone Ropeway at Sōunzan: the cable-hauled leg of the classic Hakone circuit.

name: Mount Takao Cable Car
highlight: Japan’s steepest railway (a 608 permil grade near the top), lifting hikers up Michelin three-star Mount Takao since 1927.

name: Ikoma Cable Car
highlight: Japan’s first cable railway (1918) still climbs Mount Ikoma as the country’s only double-track funicular, famed for its animal-faced cars.

name: Sakamoto Cable
highlight: Japan’s longest funicular, 2,025 m up Mount Hiei to UNESCO-listed Enryaku-ji with Lake Biwa views, running since 1927.

name: Katoomba Scenic Railway
train: 84-seat glass-roofed carriages (2013) with adjustable seat recline
highlight: The Guinness-listed steepest passenger railway on earth: a 52-degree plunge into the Jamison Valley on an 1880s coal-mine incline.

name: Wellington Cable Car
highlight: Wellington’s red icon since 1902, climbing 120 m from Lambton Quay to the Kelburn lookout. Rebuilt as a true funicular in 1979.

name: Southeastern Highspeed
highlight: Britain’s only domestic high-speed service: 225 km/h down HS1 to Ashford, then the 1844 South Eastern main line past Folkestone and under the white cliffs into Dover.

name: Southeastern Highspeed
highlight: The Javelin put Margate 86 minutes from London: HS1 at 225 km/h as far as Ashford, then the 1846 Canterbury line across east Kent to the Thanet coast.

name: Toulouse–Bayonne railway
highlight: Runs the whole width of the south-west along the foothills of the Pyrenees, opened in stages between 1861 and 1867 and still the direct way from the Atlantic to Toulouse.

name: Stralsund–Berlin railway
highlight: One of the oldest railways in Western Pomerania, built from 1863 by the Berlin-Stettin company and now the fast run down from Stralsund to Berlin.

name: Mälaren Line
highlight: Follows the northern shore of Lake Mälaren from Stockholm through Västerås to Örebro, double track most of the way and rebuilt for high-speed running in 2005.

name: Rome–Ancona railway
highlight: Crosses the Apennines sea to sea, from the Adriatic at Ancona through Foligno, Spoleto and Terni to Orte on the Rome main line.

name: Coutras–Tulle line
highlight: Single track, never electrified, opened piece by piece from 1857: the cross-country link between the Paris–Bordeaux and Orléans–Montauban main lines.

name: Haparanda Line
highlight: Sweden's only railway to the Finnish border, and freight-only from 1992 until passengers came back in 2021.

name: Danube Valley Railway
highlight: Threads the young Danube from Ulm through Blaubeuren and Riedlingen to Sigmaringen, single-tracked and largely unelectrified, and once part of the Munich–Freiburg main line.

name: Treuchtlingen–Würzburg railway
highlight: Opened in three sections from 1859 and one of Germany's oldest main lines, running through Franconia via Ansbach and Ochsenfurt into Würzburg.

name: Ruse–Kaspichan railway
highlight: The first railway ever built in Bulgaria, opened on 7 November 1866 from the Danube quays at Ruse toward the Black Sea, and still line 9 of the national network.

name: Blekinge Coast Line
highlight: The coast line through Skåne and Blekinge, opened in 1898 and now the Öresundståg run east to the naval city of Karlskrona.

name: Skåne Line
highlight: Skånebanan links eastern and western Skåne by way of Hässleholm: an 1865 railway that only got its collective name from Banverket in 1990.

name: Stendal–Uelzen railway
highlight: Mostly single track yet electrified and main-line rated, crossing the Altmark from Stendal to Uelzen with Salzwedel the one town of any size on the way.

name: Craiova–Calafat railway
highlight: A secondary single line down to the Danube, largely unelectrified, that found new purpose when the Calafat–Vidin bridge opened the way into Bulgaria.

name: Bari–Taranto railway
highlight: 104 km across the Murge plateau from Bari through Gioia del Colle to Taranto, now covered end to end by Frecciarossa in a little over an hour.

name: Pyhrn railway
highlight: Climbs from Linz over the Pyhrn Pass to Selzthal, tying the Westbahn to the Enns valley through the northern limestone Alps.

name: Brescia–Iseo–Edolo railway
highlight: Runs the length of Lake Iseo and up the Valcamonica to Edolo under the Adamello: standard gauge, single track, unelectrified, built in stages from 1885.

name: Langå–Struer railway
highlight: Central Jutland end to end: single track opened section by section from 1863, Langå to Viborg to Skive to the fjord port at Struer.

name: Bratislava–Komárno railway
highlight: Follows the Danube across the Žitný ostrov plain, and in 2012 became the first Slovak line handed over to a private operator.

name: Libourne–Le Buisson line
highlight: 97 km of single track east from the Paris–Bordeaux main line into the Périgord, opened in 1869 and still the cross-country link toward Agen and Cahors.

name: Zvolen–Vrútky railway
highlight: Slovak line 170 through the mountains north of Zvolen: the Banská Bystrica–Dolná Štubňa section alone, built 1936–40, has 22 tunnels totalling 12.2 km.

name: Košice–Prešov railway
highlight: Slovakia’s second city reached from its first: the Kaschau–Oderberg company opened the branch on 1 September 1870, north up the Hornád and off the Bohumín main line at Kysak.

name: Livorno–Florence railway
highlight: The Ferrovia Leopolda of the 1840s, still carrying Tuscany's busiest regional run from Livorno and Pisa through Pontedera and Empoli into Florence.

name: Margecany–Červená Skala railway
highlight: Single track through the Slovak Ore Mountains and along the south-east flank of the Low Tatras, climbing to the spiral and viaduct at Telgárt.

name: Main-Neckar Railway
highlight: Opened in 1846 down the Upper Rhine plain west of the Odenwald, one of Germany's oldest railways and still the local road from Frankfurt through Darmstadt and Bensheim to Heidelberg.

name: Łódź–Kutno railway
highlight: Łódź's link north to the Warsaw–Poznań main line at Kutno, through Zgierz, Ozorków and Łęczyca, part of it doubling as the city's freight ring.

name: Saar Railway
highlight: The Saarstrecke of 1858–60 follows the Saar from Trier up to Saarbrücken, one of the oldest railways in Germany and still the valley's stopping service.

name: Rennes–Saint-Malo railway
highlight: Brittany's run to the sea: 81 km from Rennes to the walled port of Saint-Malo, opened in 1864 and now covered non-stop in three quarters of an hour.

name: Valence–Moirans railway
highlight: Built by the PLM and opened on 9 May 1864 to join Valence to Grenoble, double track over two thirds of its length and electrified in the 2010s.

name: Regensburg–Ingolstadt railway
highlight: Single track but electrified up the Danube valley from Regensburg to Ingolstadt. With the Ingolstadt–Neuoffingen line, it forms the Bavarian Donautalbahn.

name: Stralsund–Rostock railway
highlight: Joins the two Hanseatic cities of the Baltic coast: single track, electrified, and rebuilt as German Unity transport project no. 1.

name: Rennes–Redon railway
highlight: The 1862 line down the Vilaine from Rennes to Redon, the shared first leg of Brittany's runs to Nantes and to Quimper.

name: Augsburg–Nördlingen railway
highlight: Part of the Ludwig South-North Railway of 1844: fast electrified track from Augsburg to Donauwörth, then the branch on to the walled crater town of Nördlingen.

name: Ystad Line
highlight: Malmö to the ferry town of Ystad across southern Scania, where the Österlen Line carries on to Simrishamn.

name: Vorarlbergbahn
highlight: Vorarlberg end to end: from Lindau on Lake Constance up the Rhine valley and the Walgau to Bludenz, where the Arlberg and Montafon lines begin.

name: Miskolc–Bánréve–Ózd railway
highlight: Branches off the Hatvan–Miskolc main line and runs up the Sajó through Bánréve to the steel town of Ózd, on the Slovak border.

name: Grenoble–Montmélian railway
highlight: Built double-track by the PLM and opened on 15 September 1864 to join Grenoble to the Savoy main line; fully electrified only in December 2013.

name: Zemitāni–Skulte railway
highlight: Latvian 1,520 mm track north from Riga to the Gulf coast at Skulte: what remains in service of the old Riga–Rūjiena and Riga–Tallinn route, cut at the Estonian border in 1992.

name: Neuchâtel–Pontarlier railway
highlight: The Franco-Suisse line of 1860 through the Val-de-Travers, single track over the Jura from Pontarlier down to the Neuchâtel lakeshore.

name: Lollandsbanen
highlight: Opened in 1874 and still crossing Lolland from Nykøbing Falster through Maribo to the shipyard town of Nakskov.

name: Prättigau Line
highlight: Metre-gauge Rhaetian track climbing the Prättigau from the Rhine valley at Landquart to the high spa town of Davos, open since 1890.

name: Engadine Line
highlight: Metre gauge down the Lower Engadine from the Albula line at Bever to the spa at Scuol-Tarasp, opened in 1913 and never joined to Austria.

name: Tallinn–Paldiski railway
highlight: Estonia's oldest railway west from Tallinn, opened in 1870 to the ice-free naval harbour at Paldiski on the Baltic.

name: Seetalbahn
highlight: Opened in 1883 by British investors down the Seetal lakes to Lucerne. For a century a roadside light railway, it was rebuilt on its own alignment in the 2000s.

name: Kystbanen
highlight: The Sound coast line of 1897, one of Denmark's busiest: Copenhagen out past the Øresund beaches to Elsinore and Kronborg.

name: Biel–La Chaux-de-Fonds railway
highlight: Single track up out of Biel through the Jura gorges to the watchmaking city of La Chaux-de-Fonds at 1,000 m, worked since 1874.

name: Frederiksværk Line
highlight: North Zealand branch line: Hillerød to Frederiksværk from 1897, on to the Kattegat ferry harbour at Hundested from 1916.

name: Arendal Line
highlight: The surviving southern stub of a line that once ran 90 km inland: electrified feeder trains down from the Sørland main line at Nelaug to the coast at Arendal.

name: Figeac–Arvant railway
highlight: 170 km of single unelectrified track across the Massif Central, tying the Brive–Toulouse main line to the Cévennes line at Arvant.

name: Székesfehérvár–Szombathely railway
highlight: Electrified but mostly single track, crossing western Hungary from Szombathely through the Bakony foothills to Székesfehérvár.

name: Tampere–Pori railway
highlight: Opened in 1895 and following the Kokemäenjoki river down to the Gulf of Bothnia, with only five intermediate stations in 132 km.

name: Vejle–Holstebro railway
highlight: Single track right across Jutland, built in pieces between 1894 and 1914 from the Vejle fjord to Herning and the west.

name: Debrecen–Füzesabony railway
highlight: Single track and unelectrified across the Great Plain, crossing the Tisza and the shallows of Lake Tisza at Tiszafüred.

name: Győr–Sopron railway
highlight: Opened on 2 January 1876 by the Raab-Oedenburg-Ebenfurth company, and still run by its successor GYSEV rather than by MÁV.

name: Jyväskylä–Pieksämäki railway
highlight: Finnish 1,524 mm track through the lake country, one stop in 79 km between the junction town of Pieksämäki and Jyväskylä.

name: Győr–Veszprém railway
highlight: The Bakonyvasút: a slow single track that leaves the Győr–Szentgotthárd line and climbs through the wooded Bakony hills to Veszprém.

name: Jura Railway
highlight: The Jurabahn of 1857 follows the Birs out of Basel into the French-speaking Jura, through Delémont and the Moutier gorges down to Biel.

name: Győr–Celldömölk railway
highlight: MÁV line 10, single track and still unelectrified, running south-west from Győr across the Kisalföld plain to the junction at Celldömölk.

name: Vercelli–Pavia railway
highlight: Opened in 1882–83 across the rice paddies between Piedmont and Lombardy, linking Vercelli to Pavia and the Po.

name: Aachen–Mönchengladbach railway
highlight: Built by the Aachen-Düsseldorf-Ruhrort company between 1852 and 1854: one of Germany's oldest lines, and still the freight road from the Ruhr to Belgium.

name: Dombóvár–Bátaszék-line
highlight: The Danube–Drava branch through southern Transdanubia, single track between the junctions at Dombóvár and Bátaszék.

name: Thur Valley Line
highlight: Switzerland's fourth-oldest railway, opened on 16 May 1855 down the Thur valley to Romanshorn, where trains once met the Lake Constance ferries.

name: Olten–Lucerne railway
highlight: Built by the Schweizerische Centralbahn and open to Lucerne since 1856: double track, electrified, and still the fast way north to Olten and Basel.

name: Szombathely–Szentgotthárd railway
highlight: The old Hungarian Western Railway toward Graz, now the through run from Szombathely to Szentgotthárd on the Austrian border.

name: Tølløse Line
highlight: A rural single track across western Zealand, joining the Northwest Line at Tølløse to the Copenhagen–Fredericia main line at Slagelse.

name: Miskolc–Tornanádaska railway
highlight: Hungarian line 94, a slow branch north of Miskolc up the Bódva valley to the Slovak border at Tornanádaska.

name: Kiskunhalas–Kiskunfélegyháza railway
highlight: Line 155 across the sandy Kiskunság between two market towns of the Great Plain, opened in 1912.

name: Bern–Neuchâtel railway
highlight: The Direkt Linie of 1901, driven almost dead straight across the Grand Marais, and still part of the shortest rail route from Bern to Paris.

name: Burgdorf–Thun railway
highlight: Opened in 1899 as the first electrified main-line railway in Europe, running from Burgdorf over Konolfingen to Thun.

name: Delémont–Delle railway
highlight: Opened in stages from 1872 through the Jura canton (Glovelier, Porrentruy, Boncourt) and over the French border to Delle.

name: Vestbanen
highlight: Nebelgrisen, the 'Nebel pig': 37 km of unelectrified West Jutland branch line from Varde out to the dune coast at Nørre Nebel.

name: Fribourg–Ins railway
highlight: Single track built by the Fribourg–Morat–Anet company, running from Fribourg past Murten and its lake to Ins in the Seeland.

name: Cadenazzo–Luino railway
highlight: Hugs the north-eastern shore of Lake Maggiore, crossing from Ticino into Italy on the way to Luino.

name: Tonkin Line
highlight: Opened in 1859 by the Ligne d'Italie, running from the Rhône at Saint-Maurice out to Lake Geneva at Le Bouveret and the French border.

name: Glarus Line
highlight: The Glarnerlinie of 1859, single track up the Linth valley under the Glärnisch and the Tödi to the road-head at Linthal.

name: Ciudad Real–Badajoz railway
highlight: 338 km west across La Mancha and the Extremadura dehesa, from Ciudad Real to the Portuguese border city of Badajoz, on track opened in 1866.

name: Linares Baeza–Almería railway
highlight: Iberian gauge from the Alcázar–Cádiz main line at Linares down through the Sierra to the Mediterranean at Almería, through the desert country the spaghetti Westerns made famous.

name: Pieksämäki–Joensuu railway
highlight: Single track, unelectrified, running east through the Finnish lakes from the junction at Pieksämäki to Joensuu near the Russian border.

name: Joensuu–Nurmes railway
highlight: Dm12 railbuses up the shore of Lake Pielinen: the rails carry on to Kontiomäki, but passenger trains have stopped at Nurmes since 1993.

name: Oulu–Kontiomäki railway
highlight: 166 km of single electrified track inland from Oulu on the Gulf of Bothnia to Kontiomäki, where five railways meet.

name: Wrocław–Poznań railway
highlight: Silesia to Wielkopolska via Leszno, opened in 1856 and now part of TEN-T corridor E59 from Scandinavia south to Vienna and Budapest.

name: Niversac–Agen railway
highlight: A slow country line opened in 1863: three and a half hours for 164 km from the Garonne at Agen up through the Périgord to the Périgueux junction at Niversac.

name: Iisalmi–Ylivieska railway
highlight: Opened in 1923 as the cross-country link between Finland's Savonia and Ostrobothnia main lines, 154 km through the forests of Kainuu.

name: Castejón–Alsasua railway
highlight: Iberian-gauge track up the Ebro and over into Navarre, opened in 1865 and still the Madrid–Basque Country road through Altsasu.

name: Palatine Ludwig Railway
highlight: The Pfälzische Ludwigsbahn of 1847, the Palatinate's main artery through Neustadt, Kaiserslautern and Homburg, and today part of the Paris–Frankfurt run.

name: Turku–Toijala railway
highlight: Finnish 1,524 mm gauge across Southwest Finland and Häme, joining the port of Turku to the Helsinki–Tampere main line at Toijala since 1876.

name: Montluçon–Saint-Sulpice-Laurières line
highlight: An 1864 cross-country line over the western edge of the Massif Central, from the Paris–Toulouse main line at Saint-Sulpice-Laurière to Montluçon.

name: Haapamäki–Seinäjoki railway
highlight: The middle section of the old Tampere–Vaasa railway of 1882, still carrying the diesel run west from the junction at Haapamäki.

name: Munich–Simbach railway
highlight: Opened on 1 May 1871 east from Munich through Markt Schwaben and Dorfen to Mühldorf and the Inn at Simbach: one of Germany's identified capacity bottlenecks.

name: Mouchard–Bourg-en-Bresse railway
highlight: Part of the Mulhouse–Besançon–Lyon route: a demanding northern section of climbs and falls through the Jura before it runs out onto the Bresse plain.

name: Tampere–Haapamäki railway
highlight: Opened in 1902 north from Tampere into the lake and forest country of central Finland, meeting the Vaasa and Jyväskylä lines at Haapamäki.

name: Iisalmi–Kontiomäki railway
highlight: Opened in 1904 through the forests of Kainuu, the northern half of the Savonia route from Iisalmi up to the five-way junction at Kontiomäki.

name: Szombathely–Nagykanizsa railway
highlight: Western Hungary north to south since 1865, from the Croatian-border junction at Nagykanizsa up past Zalaegerszeg to Szombathely.

name: Limoges–Périgueux railway
highlight: An 1861 line across the Limousin plateau, one stop in 99 km between the porcelain city of Limoges and Périgueux in the Dordogne.

name: Krustpils–Rēzekne railway
highlight: Latvian 1,524 mm track through Latgale, built as part of the Ventspils–Moscow railway and still the fast way east from the Daugava.

name: Fryksdal Line
highlight: Single track, no wires, up the Fryken lakes of Värmland from Kil to Torsby: railcars for people, timber and pulpwood for the mills.

name: Székesfehérvár–Komárom railway
highlight: Single track and still unelectrified, running from the Danube crossing at Komárom south through the Vértes foothills to Székesfehérvár.

name: Thy Line
highlight: Denmark's north-west corner by rail: 73 km from the fjord port of Struer through Thy to Thisted, open since 1882.

name: Daugavpils–Indra railway
highlight: Unelectrified 1,520 mm single track south-east from Daugavpils to Indra, the only direct rail link between Latvia and Belarus.

name: Angoulême–Saintes line
highlight: Down the Charente from Angoulême toward Saintes and the Atlantic, opened in 1867 through Cognac and its cellars.

name: Mühldorf–Freilassing railway
highlight: The south-east Bavarian cross-link of 1908, from the Salzburg border at Freilassing over the Alz and Salzach country to Mühldorf.

name: Sopron–Szombathely railway
highlight: GYSEV's own line along the Austrian border since 1865, linking Szombathely to Sopron in the corner of Hungary that voted to stay.

name: Riihimäki–Lahti railway
highlight: Opened in 1869 as the first stretch of the Riihimäki–Saint Petersburg railway, and still the connection from the Helsinki main line east to Lahti.

name: Kouvola–Kotka railway
highlight: Opened in 1890 down the Kymi river to the Gulf of Finland, ending on the quays of the port of Kotka.

name: Reims-Laon railway
highlight: 52 km across the Champagne vineyards and the Chemin des Dames country, from Reims to the cathedral on the hill at Laon.

name: Perpignan–Villefranche line
highlight: Up the Têt from the Mediterranean at Perpignan into the Pyrenean foothills, ending where the metre-gauge Train Jaune takes over at Villefranche.

name: Brig–Domodossola railway
highlight: The Swiss–Italian side of the Simplon: 41 km from Brig to Domodossola, almost half of it inside the 19.8 km Simplon Tunnel of 1906.

name: Saintes–Royan line
highlight: Half an hour down the Seudre country from Saintes to the Atlantic resort of Royan, a branch open since 1875.

name: Pápa–Csorna railway
highlight: A slow 1896 branch across the Kisalföld between the junction at Csorna and the baroque town of Pápa.

name: Kochelsee Railway
highlight: Bavarian lakes branch of 1865: from Tutzing on the Starnberger See south to the Kochelsee under the first peaks of the Alps.

name: Winterthur–Etzwilen railway
highlight: An 1875 single track north out of Winterthur through the Thur valley wine villages to Etzwilen near the Rhine.

name: Liège–Maastricht railway
highlight: Down the Meuse from Liège to Maastricht, a cross-border run open since 1861 and now worked by Arriva's Dutch regional trains.

name: Sevnica–Trebnje railway
highlight: Built in 1938 over the hills of Dolenjska, joining the Ljubljana–Novo mesto line at Trebnje to the Sava valley at Sevnica.

name: Rheinfall railway
highlight: Named for what it passes: the 1857 line from Winterthur to Schaffhausen runs along the Rhine Falls, Europe's widest waterfall.

name: Monza–Molteno railway
highlight: Brianza branch of 1911 climbing gently from Monza into the Lecco hills, twelve stops in twenty-nine kilometres.

name: Colmar–Metzeral line
highlight: Alsace's valley branch of 1868, from Colmar and its vineyards up the Fecht into the high Vosges at Metzeral.

name: Fidenza–Fornovo railway
highlight: A 1907 cut-off across the Emilian plain that lets Parma-bound freight and regional trains reach the Pontremolese line at Fornovo.

name: Huttwil–Wolhusen railway
highlight: Emmental single track of 1895, running from Huttwil down to the Little Emme and the junction at Wolhusen.

name: Magdeburg-Wittenberge railway
highlight: Double track and electrified across the Altmark, opened in 1849 by the Magdeburg-Wittenberge company and among the oldest railways in Germany.

name: Siena–Grosseto railway
highlight: Southern Tuscany at walking pace: 100 km through the Crete Senesi and the Maremma from Siena down to Grosseto, open since 1864.

name: Człuchów–Słosinko railway
highlight: PKP line 413 across the Pomeranian lakes and forests, capped at 50 km/h: an hour and a half for 84 km.

name: Kiel–Lübeck railway
highlight: Mostly single track and still without wires, joining the only two cities in Schleswig-Holstein with more than 100,000 people.

name: Haapamäki–Jyväskylä railway
highlight: Single track east from the Haapamäki junction to Jyväskylä, opened in 1897 through the lakes of central Finland.

name: Bad Kleinen–Rostock railway
highlight: Opened in 1850 by the Mecklenburg Railway Company and now part of the electrified main line that carries Berlin and Hamburg trains to the Baltic at Rostock.

name: Manzanares–Ciudad Real line
highlight: Single Iberian-gauge track across La Mancha, opened in 1861 by the MZA company and electrified today as Adif's line 522.

name: Paar Valley Railway
highlight: The Paartalbahn: 63 km of single unelectrified main line from Augsburg through Friedberg, Aichach and Schrobenhausen to Ingolstadt.

name: Saint-Étienne–Lyon railway
highlight: Continental Europe's first railway line, built by Marc and Camille Seguin between 1828 and 1833 to bring Loire coal down to the Rhône.

name: Ammersee Railway
highlight: The Ammerseebahn, single track from Mering near Augsburg past Geltendorf and the Ammersee to Weilheim under the Bavarian Alps.

name: Haller Willem
highlight: The Haller Willem climbs the Teutoburg Forest on a gradient built in 1886; the tunnel that would have eased it was left out to save money.

name: Lunéville–Saint-Dié line
highlight: Fifty km of electrified single track up the Meurthe into the Vosges, never doubled because, unlike its neighbours, it carried no strategic traffic.

name: Broye Line
highlight: Single track across Romandy's Broye valley, crossing its sister line at Payerne on the way from Lake Neuchâtel to Fribourg.

name: Österlen Line
highlight: Rebuilt from two closed Skåne railways and reopened in 2003, electrified and single track along the Österlen coast to Simrishamn.

name: Neumarkt-Sankt Veit–Landshut railway
highlight: Single track and unelectrified down the Vils valley from Neumarkt-Sankt Veit to the Isar at Landshut, open since 1883.

name: Olsztyn–Ełk railway
highlight: Across Masuria through Szczytno and Pisz: the old East Prussian line from Allenstein to Lyck, still one train's ride end to end.

name: Vilnius–Turmantas railway
highlight: Part of the 1862 Saint Petersburg–Warsaw railway, running north from Vilnius past Ignalina's lakes to the Latvian border at Turmantas.

name: Heath Railway
highlight: The Heidebahn crosses the Lüneburg Heath from Hanover to Buchholz: single track, no wires, and one of only two railways of any weight on the heath.

name: Amiens–Laon railway
highlight: Double track the whole way and still without wires, running east from Amiens through Tergnier to the hill town of Laon since 1857.

name: Vilnius–Marcinkonys railway
highlight: Another surviving arm of the Warsaw–Saint Petersburg railway, single track down through the Dzūkija pine forests to Marcinkonys.

name: Tartu-Koidula railway
highlight: One train a day each way in winter across Põlvamaa to the border station at Koidula; in summer the service carries on to Piusa.

name: Elron
highlight: How Estonian trains reach Latvia: the Baltic Railway’s 1887 branch to Valga, built to meet the Riga line, and the Riga train still runs on it.

name: Lübeck–Lüneburg railway
highlight: Single track, unelectrified, opened in sections between 1851 and 1864: one of Germany's oldest railways, from the Elbe salt town to the Baltic.

name: Line 166 (Athus–Meuse)
highlight: Up the Meuse and over the Ardennes from Dinant to Bertrix: passenger trains on the Athus–Meuse freight road between Antwerp and Basel.

name: Valencia–Alicante line
highlight: The Iberian-gauge coastal alternative to the AVE: 1,668 mm single track through Xàtiva and Villena, still worked end to end by the Euromed.

name: Alicante–Murcia line
highlight: Iberian gauge since 1884, threading the Elche palm groves and the Segura valley between two provincial capitals in under an hour.

name: Xàtiva–Alcoi railway
highlight: Iberian-gauge single track opened in 1904, climbing 64 km of viaducts and tunnels from the Xàtiva plain into the mountains at Alcoi.

name: Gäu Railway
highlight: The Stuttgart end of the Gäubahn, built by the Württemberg and Baden state railways and still the through road toward Zurich.

name: Kalwaria Zebrzydowska–Bielsko-Biała railway
highlight: Built as the Kaiser Ferdinand Northern Railway's Bielitz–Kalwaria local line, running through Wadowice under the Beskids.

name: Eiderstedt Line
highlight: Out along the Eiderstedt peninsula through Tönning and Garding to the North Sea beach at Sankt Peter-Ording, on track laid in 1854.

name: Clisson–Cholet line
highlight: Follows the Sèvre Nantaise east from Clisson to Cholet, 39 km of single unelectrified track joining two north–south main lines.

name: Münster–Rheine railway
highlight: Double track and electrified across the Münsterland, opened by the Royal Westphalian Railway Company in 1856.

name: Donauwörth–Treuchtlingen railway
highlight: Double track over the Franconian Jura, part of the trans-European core network and of the Munich–Augsburg–Nuremberg main road.

name: Lauter Valley Railway
highlight: The Lautertalbahn follows its river out of Kaiserslautern to Lauterecken, a branch the Bundesbahn planned to close in the 1980s and never did.

name: Lutterbach–Kruth line
highlight: Up the Thur valley from Mulhouse through Thann to Kruth in the high Vosges, worked by SNCF trains and the Mulhouse tram-train together.

name: Appenzell Line
highlight: Metre-gauge adhesion track from Gossau up through Appenzell to Wasserauen under the Alpstein, running continuously since 1949.

name: Neckarelz–Osterburken railway
highlight: Opened in 1866 as part of the Baden Odenwald Railway from Heidelberg to Würzburg, now double track and electrified along the edge of the Odenwald.

name: Marktoberdorf–Füssen railway
highlight: The Allgäu branch to Füssen, opened by a private local railway in 1889 and now the train that delivers visitors below Neuschwanstein.

name: Brașov–Zărnești railway
highlight: A Transylvanian branch across the Burzenland from Brașov to Zărnești, under the limestone wall of the Piatra Craiului.

name: Rostock–Tessin railway
highlight: What is left of the 1895 branch east of Rostock: trains still run to Tessin, while the track on to Tribsees has been lifted.

name: Deister Railway
highlight: The Deisterbahn of 1872 skirts the wooded Deister ridge west of Hanover, now worked as a link in the city's S-Bahn.

name: Tüßling–Burghausen railway
highlight: A short Bavarian branch to the Salzach and the longest castle complex in the world at Burghausen.

name: Lausanne–Vallorbe line
highlight: The climb from Lake Geneva into the Jura at Vallorbe: since 1870 the shortest rail route between Paris and Milan.

name: Thessaloniki–Florina
highlight: West on the 1894 Salonika–Monastir line: orchard country past Veroia, Edessa of the waterfalls, then the high lakes plateau to Florina.

name: Proastiakos Patras Π2
highlight: Eight metre-gauge kilometres north along the Gulf of Patras to Rio, under the cables of the Rio–Antirrio bridge, on track reopened for the suburban in July 2010.

name: Proastiakos Patras Π1
highlight: West out of Patras on the old metre-gauge Pyrgos line, running the beach villages of the Achaean coast to Kato Achaia, which got its trains back in February 2020.

name: Sevilla–Huelva
highlight: The 1880 MZA line west over the Guadalquivir plain and Condado vineyards to the Atlantic at Huelva, whose neo-Mudéjar terminus has stood empty since 2019 and lost its roof to a fire in 2022.

name: Ballina Branch
