highlight: Mayo’s surviving branch: half an hour down the Moy valley from Ballina to Manulla Junction, meeting the Dublin trains on the Westport line.

name: Limerick–Waterford
highlight: Ireland’s quiet cross-country line of 1854: a change of trains at Limerick Junction, then the Suir valley through Cahir and Clonmel to Waterford.

name: Limerick–Ballybrophy
highlight: The Nenagh branch, joined up in 1864: along the Shannon past Castleconnell’s rapids, then North Tipperary farmland through Nenagh and Roscrea to the mainline junction at Ballybrophy. Two through trains a day.

name: Leeds–Morecambe
highlight: The 1850 “Little North Western” the slow way out of Airedale: Bentham’s fell country, the Lune valley at Wennington, and the sands of Morecambe Bay to finish.

name: Athens–Chalkida
highlight: Athens’s other suburban artery: up the mainline past Oinoi, then the 1904 branch down to the Euripus strait at Chalkida, the gateway to Evia.

name: Proastiakos Airport Line
highlight: Port to plane on one ticket: from Piraeus through central Athens, then east along the Attiki Odos motorway median to the airport at Spata.

name: Shrewsbury–Chester
highlight: The 1848 border line between two walled towns: over Telford’s country at Chirk and the great Cefn viaduct, down the Dee valley through Wrexham to Chester.

name: Málaga–Sevilla
highlight: The slow way between Andalucía’s two great cities: up the Guadalhorce past El Chorro’s gorge, beneath the Caminito del Rey walkway, then across the campiña by Osuna and Marchena.

name: Almería–Granada
highlight: Across the high desert of the Hoya de Guadix: Almería’s palms to Granada by way of Moreda, through the badlands the spaghetti Westerns loved.

name: Jaén–Cádiz
highlight: One train across all Andalucía: olive country at Jaén, the Guadalquivir at Córdoba and Seville, sherry country at Jerez, and the Atlantic at Cádiz.

name: Jaén–Madrid
highlight: The classic climb out of Andalucía: through the Despeñaperros gorge, the old gateway pass, then straight across La Mancha to Madrid.

name: Sevilla–Zafra
highlight: North out of Seville into the Sierra Morena: cork oaks and mining country by Cazalla and Llerena to the junction town of Zafra.

name: West Wales Line
highlight: The 1856 line west: Llanelli’s sands, the Tywi at Carmarthen, then deep Pembrokeshire to the haven Nelson called the finest port in Christendom.

name: Pembroke Dock Branch
highlight: Branch line to the sea at every turn: Tenby’s walls and beaches, Saundersfoot, and the Cleddau at Pembroke Dock.

name: Fishguard Harbour Line
highlight: The boat train’s line since 1906: over the Preseli foothills to Fishguard Harbour, where the ferry sails for the Rosslare this atlas draws from the Irish side.

name: Rhymney Line
highlight: The Rhymney Railway’s own valley, opened to passengers in March 1858: out of Cardiff through the Caerphilly tunnel under the mountain, then Ystrad Mynach and Bargoed to the head of the valley at Rhymney.

name: Ebbw Vale Line
highlight: A coal line carrying people again: passenger trains ended in 1962, came back to Ebbw Vale Parkway in February 2008 and reached Ebbw Vale Town in May 2015, climbing the Ebbw valley off the Newport main line.

name: Maesteg Line
highlight: West along the South Wales main line to Bridgend, then up the Llynfi valley on Llynvi and Ogmore metals through Tondu to Maesteg. Reopened to passengers in 1992, twenty-two years after the last train.

name: Vale of Glamorgan Line
highlight: The coast road to Bridgend: through Barry and out along the Glamorgan shore past Rhoose, where the airport is, and Llantwit Major. Passenger trains stopped in June 1964 and returned in June 2005 with two new stations.

name: Borderlands Line
highlight: Wrexham to the Wirral: 1860s Wrexham, Mold and Connah’s Quay metals joined to the 1896 North Wales and Liverpool line, crossing the Dee on the Hawarden swing bridge and running on to Bidston for Liverpool.

name: EuroCity Zürich–München
highlight: Electrified through in 2020, which cut an hour off the run: out of Zurich by Winterthur and St Gallen, over the Rhine at St Margrethen, along Lake Constance through Bregenz and Lindau, then the Allgäu to Munich.

name: Intercity Vlissingen
highlight: The long way to the sea: Haarlem, Leiden, The Hague and Rotterdam, then over the Hollands Diep into Zeeland and along the Scheldt through Goes and Middelburg to Vlissingen, on rails finished in 1873.

name: Bucharest–Sofia
highlight: Two capitals in a day: south from Bucharest to the Danube, over the 1954 Friendship Bridge at Giurgiu into Ruse, then across the Bulgarian plain by Gorna Oryahovitsa and Pleven to Sofia.

name: EIC Warszawa–Szczecin
highlight: Warsaw to the Oder in four and a quarter hours, on the old Prussian main line west through Poznań, then Krzyż and Stargard to Szczecin, where Poland meets the German border.

name: Sofia–Vidin
highlight: Up the Iskar gorge, which is the reason to take it: the river cuts a canyon north out of Sofia through Svoge and Lakatnik to Mezdra, then Vratsa and the plain to the Danube at Vidin.

name: Kyiv–Chernivtsi
highlight: Overnight across western Ukraine: out of Kyiv just before nine, Lviv in the small hours, then Ivano-Frankivsk and Kolomyia to Chernivtsi by breakfast, ending on the Habsburg line of 1866.

name: Intercity Den Helder–Nijmegen
highlight: Coast to the German border in one train: from Den Helder at the tip of North Holland through Alkmaar and Amsterdam, then Utrecht, the edge of the Veluwe and Arnhem to Nijmegen on the Waal.

name: Zagreb–Vinkovci
highlight: East across Slavonia on the old Zagreb to Belgrade main line: out through Dugo Selo, the Sava plain by Novska and Slavonski Brod, then the oak country beyond Đakovo to Vinkovci.

name: Linha de Guimarães
highlight: Metre gauge until 2004, when it was rebuilt to Iberian gauge and wired: out of Porto through Ermesinde and up the Ave valley by Trofa and Santo Tirso to Guimarães, where Portugal was founded.

name: IC Antwerpen–Hasselt
highlight: An hour east from the Scheldt to the Demer: out of Antwerp through Lier, then Heist-op-den-Berg and Diest across the Campine to Hasselt, on rails joined up in the 1860s.

name: Javelin North Kent
highlight: The other Javelin to Margate: off HS1 at Ebbsfleet onto the 1846 North Kent line, past Rochester’s castle and cathedral, Faversham’s breweries, then the seaside string of Whitstable, Herne Bay and Margate.

name: Østfoldbanen: Oslo–Ski
highlight: The original 1879 Østfold line out of Oslo, hugging the fjord shore through Nordstrand and Ljan before climbing the ridge to Ski, now the all stations companion to the Blix tunnel bored beneath it.

name: Østre linje
highlight: Norway’s 1882 eastern line: through the Blix tunnel to Ski in eleven minutes, then out across the grain fields and timber towns of indre Østfold, calling at Askim and Mysen on the way to Rakkestad.

name: Bratsbergbanen
highlight: Built in 1917 to carry Norsk Hydro’s fertiliser from the Notodden works to the sea, the Bratsberg line climbs from the Telemark canal towns past Skien and crosses the Sørland main line at Nordagutu.

name: R10 Krakonoš
highlight: Rychlík from Prague across the Elbe lowlands to Hradec Králové, then up the foothills to Trutnov beneath the Krkonoše mountains.

name: RegioJet R8
highlight: RegioJet’s yellow trains on the R8: through the Moravian Gate via Přerov, on rails the Nordbahn laid toward Bohumín in 1847.

name: IC Warszawa–Lublin
highlight: The 1877 Vistula River Railroad east from Warsaw, rebuilt for 160 km/h: under two hours to Lublin’s renaissance old town.

name: IC Warszawa–Olsztyn
highlight: Off the Gdańsk main line at Działdowo, then through the wooded lake country via Nidzica and Olsztynek into Olsztyn, gateway to Masuria.

name: IC Brda
highlight: The 1862 Warsaw–Bydgoszcz Railway via the brick-gothic city of Toruń, Copernicus’s birthplace, to the Brda riverside.

name: Nadodrzanka
highlight: The Nadodrzanka: down the Oder valley through Głogów and Zielona Góra, the quiet 1870s corridor between Silesia and the Baltic.

name: R Urpín
highlight: Named for the hill above Banská Bystrica: the southern rychlík route via Levice and Zvolen into the heart of central Slovakia.

name: Zvolen–Košice railway
highlight: The southern trans-Slovak line: three hours through the karst country via Lučenec, Plešivec and Rožňava beneath medieval mining towns.

name: Railjet Wien–Venezia
highlight: One seat Vienna to Venice: over the Semmering, through the new Koralm tunnel to Klagenfurt and Villach, then the 1879 Pontebbana across the Julian Alps.

name: EC Wien–Ljubljana
highlight: The EuroCity to Slovenia on the 1857 Southern Railway: over the Semmering to Graz, the Drava at Maribor, then the Sava valley into Ljubljana.

name: IC Köln–Norddeich
highlight: DB’s seaside Intercity: down the Rhine-Ruhr, through Münster and the Emsland flats to the North Sea pier at Norddeich Mole.

name: R9 Vysočina
highlight: The slow way to Brno: the 1953-completed Vysočina highland line via Havlíčkův Brod and Žďár, the second main line between the two cities.

name: Silesian Mountain Railway
highlight: The 1867 Silesian Mountain Railway: through Wałbrzych’s coal valleys and Jelenia Góra, climbing to nearly 700 m at Szklarska Poręba under the Karkonosze.

name: Košice–Humenné railway
highlight: Eastern Slovakia’s REX corridor via Trebišov toward the Vihorlat hills; the Humenné sleeper from Prague finishes on the same rails.

name: Kék Hullám
highlight: The Kék Hullám (Blue Wave) IC along Balaton’s vineyard-clad north shore: Balatonfüred, the basalt hills of Badacsony, then inland to Tapolca.

name: ICE Frankfurt–Dresden
highlight: The Saxony ICE: Fulda’s wooded hills, Luther’s Eisenach and Erfurt, the 2015 high-speed line into Leipzig, then the Elbe plain to Dresden.

name: IC Karlsruhe–Nürnberg
highlight: The cross-country IC via the 1861 Remsbahn: Stuttgart, the Rems valley vineyards, then Aalen and Crailsheim’s hills to Nuremberg.

name: IC Poznań–Gdynia
highlight: Across Wielkopolska and Pomerania: Gniezno’s cathedral hill, Bydgoszcz, then the Vistula crossing at Tczew and the Tri-City coast to Gdynia.

name: Braunschweig–Uelzen railway
highlight: The emigrants’ road: Braunschweig via Gifhorn to Uelzen, on to the America ships at Bremen and Hamburg; single track since the war, never wired, famously Germany’s most delayed line.

name: Outback Xplorer
highlight: Weekly railcar over the Blue Mountains and out past Parkes into the saltbush: thirteen hours from Sydney Central to the silver town on the South Australian border.

name: Tshiuetin
highlight: The Labrador iron road with no highway beside it: twice a week from the St Lawrence at Sept-Îles to Schefferville, on the first railway in North America owned and run by First Nations.

name: Ravenglass & Eskdale Railway
highlight: Fifteen-inch gauge up Eskdale from the Cumbrian coast, laid for iron ore in 1875 and run since as a miniature main line that Cumbria calls La’al Ratty.

name: Kandertalbahn
highlight: Sunday steam up the Kandertal from the Rhine plain at Haltingen to Kandern, the 1895 branch kept running by the society that saved it.

name: Mátravasút (Mátra Forest Railway)
highlight: Seven-sixty gauge out of Gyöngyös into the Mátra hills: a 1920s timber railway carrying holidaymakers to Mátrafüred behind an Mk48 in open-sided coaches.

name: ICE Hamburg–Binz
highlight: The Rügen through train: out of Hamburg past Schwerin and Rostock to Stralsund, over the Rügendamm and on to the chalk coast at Binz.

name: ICE Dortmund–Oberstdorf
highlight: The Ruhr to the Allgäu in one train: Dortmund, the Rhine gorge past the Lorelei, Mannheim and Ulm, then up the Iller valley to Oberstdorf under the Alps.

name: IC Gera–Düsseldorf
highlight: East Thuringia to the Rhine: Gera and Jena, Erfurt and Eisenach under the Wartburg, then Kassel, the Ruhr and Düsseldorf.

name: IC Leipzig–Norddeich
highlight: Saxony to the North Sea ferry pier: Leipzig, Magdeburg and Hannover, then Bremen and the East Frisian flats to the quayside at Norddeich Mole.

name: IC Leipzig–Warnemünde
highlight: Leipzig to the Baltic beach: Halle and Magdeburg, the Stendal cut-off and Schwerin, then Rostock and out to the pier at Warnemünde.

name: EN Slovakia / Chopin
highlight: Overnight between two capitals: out of Prague past Pardubice and Olomouc, over the border to Katowice, then the fast Central Trunk line into Warsaw by breakfast.

name: Eurotunnel Le Shuttle
highlight: Drive on at Folkestone, drive off at Calais: thirty five minutes under the Channel on the shuttle that carries the cars, and the only fixed link between Britain and the continent.

name: Vereina Car Shuttle
highlight: Metre gauge under the Silvretta: cars loaded at Selfranga near Klosters and carried through the 19 km Vereina tunnel to the Engadine, open when the Flüela pass is shut.

name: Tauernschleuse
highlight: Salzburg to Carinthia without the pass: the car shuttle through the 1909 Tauern tunnel, hourly under the Alpine main ridge from Böckstein to Mallnitz.

name: EC Wawel
highlight: The EuroCity across Poland: Berlin and the Oder, Wrocław and Opole, the Silesian cities and Kraków, then on east to Przemyśl at the Ukrainian border.

name: Bregenzerwaldbahn (Wälderbähnle)
highlight: All that is left of the 760 mm line to Bregenz: five kilometres of the Wälderbähnle between Bezau and Schwarzenberg, worked by steam and diesel through the Bregenzerwald on summer weekends.

name: Intercity
highlight: West Flanders end to end: out of the dunes at De Panne past Veurne and Diksmuide, then Tielt and Deinze to Ghent, on the line that finally reached the coast in 1870.

name: Intercity
highlight: East across the Campine heath from Antwerp, through Lier, Herentals, Geel and Mol to Hamont in the far corner of Limburg, on rails completed in 1879.

name: Intercity
highlight: Flanders’ two great cities in an hour, straight through the Waasland at Sint-Niklaas and Lokeren, on a line that reached Ghent in 1847 but Antwerp’s own stations only in 1970, through the Kennedy tunnel under the Scheldt.

name: Intercity
highlight: The long way to the sea: from the airport out to Denderleeuw, then Oudenaarde, Kortrijk and Roeselare through the Flemish Ardennes before Bruges and Ostend.

name: Intercity
highlight: Down the oldest railway on the Continent, Brussels to Mechelen in 1835, then the 1843 line south past Nivelles into the Sambre coalfield at Charleroi.

name: Intercity
highlight: Forty-six minutes down the Meuse, Liège to Namur under the cliffs and citadels of the valley, on the line the Namur to Liège company opened along the riverbank in 1850.

name: IC Warszawa–Terespol
highlight: Warsaw east to the Bug on the 1866 Terespol railway, the third line built in Congress Poland, running through Siedlce and Biała Podlaska to the Belarusian frontier.

name: Piła–Szczecin railway
highlight: Across Pomerania on a railway the Prussians finished in 1895 and Poland gave up on in 2000: through trains came back to Wałcz and Choszczno in 2012, five pairs a day.

name: Szczecin–Świnoujście railway
highlight: Szczecin to the Baltic across Wolin island, over the Dziwna and through Międzyzdroje to the ferry berths at Świnoujście, on rails that reached the Świna in 1900.

name: IC Olsztyn–Elbląg
highlight: Warmia end to end, Olsztyn through Morąg to Elbląg and the Vistula Lagoon, on a line that reached Olsztyn from Bogaczewo in August 1883.

name: Inowrocław–Olsztyn railway
highlight: Kuyavia to Masuria across the Vistula at Toruń, then Iława and Ostróda to Olsztyn, on the Prussian trunk that joined Poznań to East Prussia in 1873.

name: Sierpc–Nowy Dwór railway
highlight: A Mazovian branch line: Sierpc down the Wkra valley to Nasielsk, then Modlin and Nowy Dwór, on a First World War military narrow gauge regauged and opened properly in 1924.

name: Lublin–Zamość railway
highlight: Lublin south east to Zamość and its Renaissance old town, through Rejowiec and the Wieprz valley, on the section of the Rejowiec to Hrebenne line opened in 1916.

name: Katowice–Zwardoń railway
highlight: Out of the Silesian coalfield into the Beskids: Katowice through Tychy and Bielsko-Biała to Żywiec and the Slovak border at Zwardoń, a line completed piece by piece to 1912.

name: Dęblin–Łuków railway
highlight: Dęblin to Łuków across the Lublin plain, on rails that took sixty years to join up: Łuków reached Stawy in 1876 and the last stretch into Dęblin waited until 1935.

name: Kutno–Płock railway
highlight: Kutno north to Płock and the Vistula, on a line opened on the last day of 1925, the bridge over the river into the city following in 1938.

name: RE 3 Dresden–Hof
highlight: Saxony corner to corner: out of Dresden up the Tharandt ramp, then Freiberg, Chemnitz, Zwickau and the Vogtland to Hof, on a chain of lines the Freiberg link joined up in 1869.

name: RE 6 Chemnitz–Leipzig
highlight: An hour between Saxony’s two biggest cities, Chemnitz to Leipzig by way of Geithain and Borna, on a line opened in April 1872.

name: RB 45 Chemnitz–Elsterwerda
highlight: North out of Chemnitz down the Zschopau valley to Döbeln and Riesa on the Elbe, then on to Elsterwerda, joining a railway of 1852 to one of 1875.

name: RB 1 Zwickau–Kraslice
highlight: Out of the Zwickau coalfield into the Vogtland hills and over the Czech border above Klingenthal to Kraslice, on rails a coal railway company opened in November 1875.

name: RB 59 Gammertingen–Schelklingen
highlight: Across the Swabian Alb at sixty kilometres an hour: Gammertingen to Engstingen and Münsingen, then down to Schelklingen and the Danube, on branch lines opened in 1901.

name: R-1 Madrid–Ávila
highlight: Out of Madrid past El Escorial and over the Guadarrama to Ávila and its complete medieval walls, on the main line to the French border built between 1860 and 1864.

name: Oradea–Püspökladány railway
highlight: Over the Hungarian border on rails the Tisza Railway Company put into service on 22 April 1858, still the way out of Oradea onto the Great Plain at Püspökladány.

name: Hanko line
highlight: Finland’s first private railway, opened in 1873 and paid for by St Petersburg merchants who wanted an ice free winter port: forty minutes down the branch from Karjaa to Hanko.

name: RE 2 Liberec–Dresden
highlight: Bohemia into Saxony on the Lusatian branches: Liberec down the Neisse to Zittau, then Ebersbach and Bischofswerda, on a chain the Oberoderwitz link completed in October 1879.

name: S6 Lienz–Villach
highlight: Down the Drau from East Tyrol into Carinthia, Lienz past Oberdrauburg and Spittal to Villach, on the original Drautalbahn of 20 November 1871: an S-Bahn since 2015, renumbered S6 in December 2025.

name: S4 Villach–Hermagor
highlight: South out of Villach to Arnoldstein, then west up the Gail valley to Hermagor, on a branch opened on 11 August 1894 and ridden by 310 people on its first train.

name: Tunis–Annaba
train: SNCFT first and second class coaches
highlight: Tunis to Béja, Jendouba and Ghardimaou, then over the border to Souk Ahras and Annaba: the 1884 Bône-Guelma link, silent from 1995 until the first train ran again on 11 August 2024.

name: Nanning–Hanoi International
highlight: Out of Nanning by night through Chongzuo and Pingxiang, over the border at Đồng Đăng, down to Gia Lâm in Hanoi: through since 1955, stopped in 2020, running again from 25 May 2025.

name: Pitești–Craiova railway
highlight: Opened on 9 May 1878, six years after the line from Bucharest had reached Pitești, and still an unelectrified single track running west across the Olt to Craiova.

name: Varna–Shumen railway
highlight: The last 24 km into Shumen opened on 20 June 1895; everything east of Kaspichan is the first railway built in what is now Bulgaria, the Ruse to Varna line of 1866.

name: Niš–Zaječar railway
highlight: The Timok valley line, finished in 1922 by Russian emigre labour through nineteen tunnels in the Svrljig gorge, and still the only rail link between Niš and the eastern border country.

name: R Zakarpatia
highlight: The daily crossing out of Transcarpathia into the European gauge, over the Tisza at Cierna nad Tisou on a line whose last section opened on 22 October 1873.

name: Kraljevo–Rudnica railway
highlight: Up the Ibar valley past Mataruska Banja and Josanicka Banja, on rails completed in 1931 to carry ore north out of the Ibar mines, and the only atlas line for a hundred kilometres in any direction.

name: Chiltern Main Line
highlight: The other main line from London to Birmingham: finished in 1910, when the Bicester cut-off shortened it by thirty kilometres and let the Great Western match its rival on two hours.

name: West Coastway line
highlight: Five companies built this coast road in rails between 1840 and 1889; the last of it runs out over the water on piles into Portsmouth Harbour, opened on 2 October 1876.

name: Hatvan–Somoskőújfalu railway
highlight: Coal from Salgótarján is why it exists: Hatvan to the pits opened on 9 May 1867, and the single track on through Somoskőújfalu to Losonc followed in 1871.

name: L2 Děčín–Liberec
highlight: Four companies laid it in pieces from 1869 onwards; the last link opened on 16 September 1900, climbing to Liberec through five tunnels and over the 30 m viaduct at Novina.

name: Monforte de Lemos–A Coruña railway
highlight: For seventy years the only railway between Galicia and the meseta: Lugo to A Coruña opened on 10 October 1875, and the last stretch east of Monforte on 4 September 1883.

name: Baja–Kiskunhalas railway
highlight: Trianon cut two branch lines in half and Hungary joined the stumps: the Baja end opened on 8 January 1885, the Kiskunhalas end on 31 October 1903.

name: Skövde–Nässjö railway
highlight: The Jönköpingsbanan was the Southern main line’s own way north, finished on 1 December 1864; ten years later a shorter line through Katrineholm took its traffic away.

name: Sierpc–Toruń railway
highlight: One of the last railways the Second Republic built: eighty kilometres laid between 1935 and 1937, and the Drwęca bridge at Lubicz was the first in Poland to carry welded girders.

name: Varna–Burgas railway
highlight: Begun in 1916, abandoned, and finished in the war: Karnobat to Komunari opened in 1942 and the last stretch down the Kamchia valley in 1943, joining Bulgaria’s two Black Sea cities directly.

name: Valladolid–Puebla de Sanabria railway
highlight: Thirty years of building, some of it by Republican prisoners at forced labour: the climb from Zamora to Puebla de Sanabria opened on 23 September 1952.

name: Fossano–San Giuseppe di Cairo railway
highlight: The 1874 road to Savona ran the long way round through Bra; this double track shortcut by way of Mondovì and Ceva replaced it in 1933.

name: Donauuferbahn
highlight: Mauthausen to Grein opened on 4 July 1898 and the state line on through the Strudengau in 1909; trains now turn at St. Nikola-Struden, where the rest of the Danube line was given up in 2019.

name: Békéscsaba–Salonta railway
highlight: The Alföld to Fiume company opened it on 14 September 1871 and then went broke; Trianon cut the line in two, but nobody lifted the rails and the crossing still works.

name: Číčenice–Nové Údolí railway
highlight: Prachatice was reached in 1893, Volary in 1899 and the Bavarian border in 1910; through trains to Passau stopped in 1951 and the rails past Nové Údolí are now pushed by hand.

name: Évora–Beja railway
highlight: Two railways of the 1860s meet at Casa Branca: the branch up to Évora opened on 14 September 1863, and the main line reached Beja on 15 February 1864.

name: Almtalbahn
highlight: Wels built it to keep the Almtal from Lambach: the branch from Sattledt opened in 1901, owned by a local company until 1942 and run by the state railway from the first day.

name: Neusiedler Seebahn
highlight: It opened on 19 December 1897 with all 109 km of it inside Hungary; Trianon moved the northern part into Austria in 1921, and trains have crossed the border at Pamhagen ever since.

name: Biella–Novara railway
highlight: Mussolini opened it on 18 May 1939 and no train ran for fourteen months, because the rolling stock was not ready; promised electric in 1925, it never was, and the state took it over in 1961.

name: Chivasso–Casale Monferrato railway
highlight: A third class line under the Baccarini law of 1879, built to reach the Monferrato from the main line at Chivasso: the stretch from Castelrosso to Casale Popolo opened on 30 April 1887.

name: Markarydsbanan
highlight: The Southern main line nearly came this way in the 1850s and went east instead; two small companies built it anyway, Hässleholm to Vittsjö in 1890 and on to Markaryd in 1892.

name: Vác–Balassagyarmat railway
highlight: Two railways meet at Drégelypalánk: the Ipoly valley line reached Balassagyarmat on 15 August 1891, and the line south through the Börzsöny to Vác carried its first train on 11 July 1909.

name: Hausruckbahn
highlight: The northern half of the Salzkammergutbahn, opened on 23 October 1877 by the Crown Prince Rudolf company to bring Hausruck coal down to the salt pans of Ebensee and Ischl.

name: Innkreisbahn
highlight: Neumarkt-Kallham to Braunau opened on 20 December 1870 and the bridge over the Inn to Simbach on 1 June 1871; from 1883 to 1897 the Orient Express took this way between Vienna and Munich.

name: Linzer Lokalbahn
highlight: Electric from the start: Waizenkirchen to Peuerbach opened in 1908, the link on to Eferding and Linz on 16 December 1912, and Stern & Hafferl have run it since 1 January 1913.

name: Franz-Josefs-Bahn
highlight: The first 22 km of the line to Gmünd and Prague: the Vienna end opened in 1870, once the delayed stretch in from Eggenburg was finished, and ran as part of the Stadtbahn from 1898 to 1925.

name: EBOE Elmshorn–Ulzburg
highlight: Elmshorn to Barmstedt opened as a light railway on 15 July 1896; the Barmstedt to Oldesloe company carried it on to Ulzburg on 9 June 1907, and the AKN has run it since 1981.

name: Biel–Bern railway
highlight: Bern to Zollikofen opened on 16 June 1857 as part of the Centralbahn line to Olten; the Bernese state railway carried it on over Lyss to Biel in 1864.

name: Odsherredsbanen
highlight: Point one of the great railway act of 1894: Holbæk county took the concession on 6 May 1896, and the line up the peninsula to Nykøbing opened on 18 May 1899.

name: Østbanen
highlight: The East Zealand line began service on 1 July 1879, Køge through Hårlev to the sea at Faxe Ladeplads; the trains from Køge still divide at Hårlev, one half for the coast and the other for Rødvig.

name: Gribskovbanen
highlight: Built in 1880 to carry timber out of the Gribskov forest as far as Græsted; the line reached the sea at Gilleleje on 14 May 1896, and its passengers have called it the Pig ever since.

name: Parikkala–Savonlinna railway
highlight: The Savonlinna line was built from Elisenvaara on the Karelian railway: Punkaharju was reached in November 1906 and the whole line on 1 February 1908; the junction it started from is now in Russia.

name: Tjustbanan
highlight: Västervik to Åtvidaberg was laid in 1879 as an 891 mm narrow gauge line; the link to Bjärka-Säby in 1906 joined it to Linköping, and the whole of it was widened to standard gauge in 1964.

name: Laskowice–Czersk railway
highlight: A Prussian act of 20 July 1902 ordered it, and the 55 km from Laskowice to Czersk opened on 2 October 1906; the stretch beyond to Bąk came in 1928 to feed the building of the coal trunk line.

name: Czersk–Tuchola railway
highlight: A piece of the coal trunk line built to reach the new port at Gdynia without crossing the Free City of Danzig: the whole Bydgoszcz to Gdynia stretch opened on 9 November 1930.

name: Catania–Caltagirone railway
highlight: Valsavoia to Scordia opened in November 1889 and the whole climb to Caltagirone on 31 October 1892; the 1979 extension to Gela has been shut since a viaduct collapsed, reopening promised for 2026.

name: Ponitran Prievidza–Bratislava
highlight: Down the Nitra valley on the StEG line of 1876 to 1896 and across to the Váh at Leopoldov on the link of 1898 that first gave Prievidza a fast train to Bratislava.

name: Zaragoza–Barcelona by Caspe
highlight: MZA’s second way from Zaragoza to the sea, built to cut out Lleida: Reus to Móra opened in 1891, Caspe was reached in 1893, the line was complete in 1894 and carried its first trains in 1895.

name: Medgidia–Tulcea railway
highlight: Begun in 1911, stopped by the war, opened to Babadag on 1 October 1925 and finished on 25 March 1938, when Tulcea, the last county town in Romania without a railway, got its first train.

name: R11 České Budějovice–Brno
highlight: Three railways end to end: the Franz Josef line to Veselí from 1871, the Bohemian transversal on to Jihlava from 1887, and the line through Třebíč to Brno, whose middle section opened in June 1886.

name: Sp Strakonice–Tábor
highlight: Opened in 1889 across South Bohemia: out of the Otava valley at Strakonice, through Písek, over the Vltava at Červená and past the stone viaducts above Milevsko to Tábor.

name: Târgu Jiu–Craiova railway
highlight: Filiași to Craiova is the 1878 line; the branch up the Jiu opened in two pieces in 1888, to Cărbunești and then to Târgu Jiu, which stayed the end of the railway for another 27 years.

name: Palermo–Trapani railway
highlight: The long way round the west of Sicily, by Castelvetrano, Mazara and Marsala: the through line was finished on 5 June 1881, and since the short route by Milo closed in 2013 it is the only one.

name: Maubeuge–Charleroi railway
highlight: Charleroi to the French frontier at Erquelinnes opened on 6 November 1852, and the Nord company’s line from Saint-Quentin met it there on 11 August 1855, on the old main road from Paris to Brussels.

name: c2c Shoeburyness–London
highlight: The Tilbury company reached Shoeburyness in 1884 and finished its direct line through Upminster to a re-sited Pitsea in 1886, the way the stopping trains from the sea to Fenchurch Street run today.

name: Chiltern Marylebone–Aylesbury Vale Parkway
highlight: Marylebone opened on 15 March 1899, the last main line terminus London built for a century; the train runs out over the old Metropolitan and Great Central road to a station opened on 14 December 2008.

name: Dartmouth Steam Railway
highlight: The Kingswear branch of 1864, sold by British Rail to the Dart Valley company in 1972: steam from Paignton over Goodrington Sands and along the Dart estuary to Kingswear, for the ferry to Dartmouth.

name: North Norfolk Railway
highlight: The Poppy Line: the last stretch of the Midland & Great Northern in Norfolk, carrying passengers again since July 1975, from the seaside at Sheringham past Weybourne to Holt.

name: Llangollen Railway
highlight: Ten miles of the Great Western’s Ruabon–Barmouth line, closed in 1965: volunteers reopened Llangollen station in 1975 and relaid the Dee valley mile by mile, reaching a new station at Corwen in 2023.

name: Epping Ongar Railway
highlight: The Central line’s lost end: London Underground closed Epping to Ongar in 1994, and heritage steam and diesel have run it again since 2012, from Ongar through North Weald to the edge of Epping Forest.

name: Embsay & Bolton Abbey Steam Railway
highlight: Four miles of the Midland’s Skipton–Ilkley line, closed in 1965 and reopened by volunteers in 1981, with trains back into Bolton Abbey station, for the priory estate, since 1997.

name: Dean Forest Railway
highlight: The Severn & Wye’s line into the Forest of Dean, rebuilt by volunteers: passenger trains since 1991, down to Lydney Junction in 1995 and up through the woods to Parkend.

name: Lakeside & Haverthwaite Railway
highlight: The Furness Railway’s 1869 branch to Windermere, reopened in 1973: three and a half miles of steam from Haverthwaite to Lakeside, where trains still connect with the lake steamers.

name: Bure Valley Railway
highlight: Norfolk’s 15-inch-gauge railway, laid in 1990 on the old East Norfolk trackbed: nine miles from the Broads at Wroxham, over the River Bure and under the A140 by tunnel, to Aylsham.

name: Chinnor & Princes Risborough Railway
highlight: A surviving piece of the Great Western’s Watlington branch at the foot of the Chilterns, reopened to passengers in 1994 and reconnected to the main line at Princes Risborough in 2016.

name: Caledonian Railway (Brechin)
highlight: Four miles of the Aberdeen Railway’s 1840s line between Brechin’s preserved terminus and Bridge of Dun, worked by volunteers every summer since 1993.

name: Cholsey & Wallingford Railway
highlight: The Great Western’s 1866 Wallingford branch, kept alive into preservation by the town’s maltings traffic: two and a half miles from Wallingford to the main line at Cholsey.

name: Gwili Railway
highlight: Wales’ first standard-gauge heritage railway, reopened in 1978 on the Carmarthen–Aberystwyth line, the last in Wales to lose Brunel’s broad gauge, and now four and a half miles up the Gwili valley.

name: Kirklees Light Railway
highlight: A 15-inch-gauge railway opened in 1991 on the Lancashire & Yorkshire’s Clayton West branch: through Skelmanthorpe and the 511-yard Shelley Woodhouse tunnel, with Emley Moor mast in view.

name: Leighton Buzzard Light Railway
highlight: Built in 1919 to carry sand from the Bedfordshire quarries and running passenger trains since 1968: two-foot-gauge industrial steam and diesel from Page’s Park to Stonehenge Works.

name: Strathspey Railway
highlight: Steam since 1978 on a preserved stretch of the Highland Railway main line, one of only a handful of former main lines saved in Britain: from Aviemore through Boat of Garten to Broomhill.

name: Volk’s Electric Railway
highlight: The world’s oldest operating electric railway: Magnus Volk opened it on Brighton seafront in August 1883, and its cars still run along the beach from Aquarium to Black Rock.

name: Manx Electric Railway
highlight: The oldest electric tramway whose original cars are still in service: 1890s tramcars on the coast line from Douglas to Laxey and, since 1899, over the cliffs to Ramsey.

name: Snaefell Mountain Railway
highlight: Wooden electric cars of 1895 climb five miles from Laxey to the 621 m summit of Snaefell, the Isle of Man’s highest point, braking on a Fell centre rail.

name: Glenbrook Vintage Railway
highlight: Steam on the old Waiuku branch south of Auckland, run by volunteers since 1977: a 7.4 km line from Glenbrook to Victoria Avenue that carries up to 30,000 passengers a season.

name: Hornbækbanen
highlight: North Zealand’s coast line: Elsinore out past the Øresund bathing towns to Hornbæk from 1906, and on to Gilleleje from July 1916.

name: Østbanen
highlight: Every station on it was drawn by Heinrich Wenck: the East Zealand line of 1879 across Stevns to the chalk cliffs at Rødvig, rebuilt and reopened in October 2024.

name: Tisvildeleje branch
highlight: The Gribskovbanen’s western arm: built in 1880 to bring timber out of the Gribskov forest, on to Helsinge in 1897 and to the Kattegat dunes at Tisvildeleje in 1924.

name: Utrecht–Rotterdam railway
highlight: The Rhenish Railway Company built it between 1855 and 1858; after the Maas station was bombed out of Rotterdam in 1940 the city end was rebuilt on an embankment and reopened in 1953.

name: Santhià–Biella railway
highlight: Inaugurated on 8 September 1856 with the public works minister aboard the special from Turin: 27 km down from the Biellese wool towns to the Turin–Milan main line at Santhià.

name: Leamington–Stratford line
highlight: The Stratford-on-Avon Railway opened its branch from Hatton on 9 October 1860; Chiltern trains still use it to reach Shakespeare’s town off the Birmingham–Oxford main line.

name: Intercity
highlight: The Louvain-to-Charleroi company opened its whole route in 1855, Leuven to Wavre in February and the last stretch into the Sambre coalfield that August; the IC-24 still runs it end to end.

name: West Friesland line
highlight: Schiphol and Amsterdam at one end, then the Hollandsche IJzeren’s branch of 1884 north through Purmerend into West Friesland, extended past Hoorn in 1885.

name: Koleje Dolnośląskie D25
highlight: Most of the old Breslau–Berlin trunk, in its 1875 alignment through Żagań: a single Lower Silesian sprinter crosses the Nysa at Zasieki and runs 189 km to Wrocław.

name: EuroCity Via Regia
highlight: Named for the medieval road it shadows: the EuroCity takes the Oberlausitz company’s line of 1874 and crosses at Horka, a border that carried no scheduled passenger trains for decades.

name: LTG Link
highlight: The old Tilsit–Memel line of 1875 along the edge of the Nemunas delta, joined at Klaipėda to the German military railway of 1915 up to Kretinga; trains came back to the Šilutė stretch in 2018.

name: Mardi Gras Service
highlight: The Gulf Coast’s first passenger trains since Hurricane Katrina: from August 2025 two a day have run from New Orleans along the Mississippi shore through Bay St. Louis, Gulfport and Biloxi to Mobile.

name: Illinois Zephyr & Carl Sandburg
highlight: America’s longest continuously running state-sponsored train: the Illinois Zephyr has run since November 1971, joined by the Carl Sandburg in 2006, across the prairie to Quincy on the Mississippi.

name: VIA Senneterre
highlight: A flag-stop train into the Abitibi bush three times a week: 13½ hours from Montreal past hunting and fishing clubs listed as request stops, to Senneterre, whose station opened in 1914.

name: Wairarapa Connection
highlight: Through the 8.8 km Remutaka Tunnel of 1955, New Zealand’s longest until 1978: rebuilt British Mark 2 carriages behind a KiwiRail diesel link Masterton and Wellington five times each weekday.

name: Bairnsdale line
highlight: Across Gippsland from Melbourne: three VLocity trains a day pass the Latrobe Valley’s coal towns to Bairnsdale, reached by rail in 1888; beyond Sale the trains stopped in 1993 and returned in 2004.

name: Hunter Line
highlight: Australia’s last regular steam passenger trains ran here until July 1971. Railcars now take the Hunter River Railway Company’s line of 1857 up the valley from Newcastle to Scone.

name: Armidale Xplorer
highlight: Up the Great Northern to the New England tableland, reached at Armidale in 1883: a daily Xplorer climbs eight hours from Sydney through the Hunter Valley and over the Liverpool Range.

name: Kounotori
highlight: Named in 2011 for the storks bred back into the wild at Toyooka: a limited express from Shin-Osaka through the Tamba hills and down the San’in line to the hot-spring town of Kinosaki.

name: Etsumi-Hoku Line
highlight: The Kuzuryū Line, completed in 1972: one-car KiHa 120s climb from Fukui through the castle town of Ōno to a dam lake, the last stretch still worked with a single staff, one of two left on JR.

name: AREX Express
highlight: Non-stop since December 2010 from Seoul Station, where some airlines check passengers in and through immigration, to Incheon Airport over the lower deck of the Yeongjong Bridge.

name: Banja Luka–Doboj railway
highlight: One of the last lines built by Yugoslavia’s youth work brigades, opened in 1951, from Banja Luka up the Vrbanja valley to Doboj. Rebuilt for 120 km/h in 2018; a daily train since December 2025.

name: Macomer–Nuoro railway
highlight: Nuoro’s only railway: the narrow-gauge line reached the town in February 1889, and ARST railcars still run down it to the main line at Macomer several times each weekday.

name: Banyubiru
highlight: On Indonesia’s first railway: the Dutch NIS company’s line out of Semarang reached Solo in February 1870, and the Banyubiru runs it twice a day through Gundih between Solo Balapan and Semarang Tawang.

name: Batara Kresna Railbus
highlight: Down the middle of Solo’s main street on an old tramway’s track, then out on the extension of 1922 to Wonogiri; since February 2025 a faster railcar takes about an hour, not two.

name: Varna–Dobrich railway
highlight: Built to carry Dobruja’s harvest to the sea: the branch from Devnya reached Dobrich in 1910, and five BDŽ trains a day still link the town with the port of Varna.

name: Nador–Taourirt line
highlight: Opened by King Mohammed VI in July 2009: a new railway from the port of Beni Ensar, under Nador in a 3 km tunnel and south across the plain to Taourirt on the Fez–Oujda main line.

name: IC Łempicka
highlight: Lublin to Wrocław the long way round, through Radom, Kielce and Częstochowa, then west across Silesia to Opole and the Oder; the Częstochowa to Kielce link, opened in 1911, was the last piece of the route.

name: IC Kasztelan
highlight: Kraków to Hrubieszów near the Ukrainian border, by Tarnów, Mielec and Stalowa Wola, then east through Biłgoraj and Zwierzyniec to Zamość and its Renaissance old town; the line from Stalowa Wola to Biłgoraj was only completed in 1976.

name: Intercity
highlight: From Poperinge’s hop fields through Ypres, then along the French border by Wervik and Menen to Kortrijk, Ghent and Antwerp; the last link, the rail tunnel under the Scheldt, opened in 1970.

name: Palermo–Catania railway
highlight: Across the middle of Sicily from Catania, up by Enna and the old sulphur country of Caltanissetta and down to the Tyrrhenian coast at Palermo; the line was complete only when the Marianopoli tunnel opened in 1885.

name: RE 7 Erfurt–Würzburg
highlight: From Erfurt over the Thuringian Forest through the 3 km Brandleite tunnel under the Rennsteig, down by Suhl and Grimmenthal into Franconia and on by Schweinfurt to Würzburg; the climb and the tunnel opened in 1884.

name: Glasgow South Western Line
highlight: The other line from Carlisle to Glasgow: over the border at Gretna, by Annan and Dumfries, up Nithsdale to Kilmarnock, and in by Barrhead on the joint line opened in 1873.

name: Franz-Josefs-Bahn
highlight: Vienna’s line to the Waldviertel: from the Franz-Josefs-Bahnhof along the Danube to Tulln, up by Eggenburg and across the forest plateau to Gmünd and over the Czech border to České Velenice; the Vienna end opened in 1870.

name: West of England line
highlight: The other way to Exeter: from Waterloo by Woking and Basingstoke, then west by Andover, Salisbury, Sherborne and Yeovil Junction, much of it on single track, to Exeter Central and down to St Davids, reached in 1862.

name: Stranraer line
highlight: From Stranraer on Loch Ryan over the moors by Barrhill, the only station left between there and Girvan, then along the Firth of Clyde by Ayr and Troon to Kilmarnock; the line through the hills opened in 1877.

name: Padua–Belluno railway
highlight: From Padua across the Venetian plain by Castelfranco and Montebelluna into the Piave valley at Feltre and on to Belluno beneath the Dolomites; the line that gave Belluno its railway opened on 10 November 1886.

name: RE 3 Saarbrücken–Frankfurt
highlight: From Saarbrücken by Neunkirchen and St. Wendel down the Nahe valley past Idar-Oberstein and Kirn to Bad Kreuznach, then along the Rhine to Mainz and over to Frankfurt; the Nahe valley railway was complete in 1860.

name: Pau–Bedous railway
highlight: From Pau by Oloron-Sainte-Marie up the Aspe valley into the Pyrenees to Bedous, the first stretch of the old line to Canfranc and Spain; trains reached Bedous in 1914, stopped in 1980 and came back on 26 June 2016.

name: Bayonne–Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port railway
highlight: Up the Nive valley from Bayonne by Cambo-les-Bains into the Basque hills to Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, where pilgrims set out over the Pyrenees to Roncesvalles; the last stretch, from Ossès, opened on 11 December 1898.

name: RB 55 Munich–Bayrischzell
highlight: The Bayerische Regiobahn from Munich by Holzkirchen to the shore of the Schliersee and up the Leitzach valley under the Wendelstein to Bayrischzell; the last stretch, from Fischbachau, opened on 1 October 1911.

name: Yorkshire Coast Line
highlight: From Hull by Beverley and Driffield to Bridlington, then along the Yorkshire coast by Filey to Scarborough; the last link, from Bridlington to Filey, opened on 20 October 1847.

name: Hastings line
highlight: From Charing Cross through the North Downs by the Sevenoaks tunnel to Tonbridge, then over the High Weald by Tunbridge Wells and Battle to the sea at Hastings; London trains have run this way since the Sevenoaks line opened in 1868.

name: Limoges–Ussel railway
highlight: From Limoges up the Vienne valley by Eymoutiers onto the Plateau de Millevaches, the high moorland of the Limousin, and down by Meymac to Ussel; the stretch from Eymoutiers to Meymac, opened on 8 October 1883, completed the line.

name: RE 5 Cuxhaven–Hamburg
highlight: Along the lower Elbe from the North Sea port of Cuxhaven by Otterndorf, Stade and Buxtehude to Harburg and over the river into Hamburg; the railway reached Cuxhaven in 1881.

name: Svendborgbanen
highlight: Across Funen from Svendborg, the harbour for the ferries to Ærø and the small islands of the South Funen archipelago, by Kværndrup and Ringe to Odense; the line opened in July 1876.

name: Givet–Charleville railway
highlight: Up the Meuse through the Ardennes from Givet, at the tip of the French salient into Belgium, by Fumay, Revin and Nouzonville to Charleville-Mézières; the line reached Givet on 28 April 1862.

name: Empire Builder (Portland section)
highlight: The Empire Builder’s Portland half: it leaves the Seattle cars at Spokane in the night and follows the Columbia River from Pasco down its gorge to Portland, a section Amtrak brought back in 1981.

name: Lake Shore Limited (Boston section)
highlight: The Lake Shore Limited’s Boston cars, split from the New York train at Albany–Rensselaer, cross the Berkshires by Pittsfield and Springfield on the old Boston and Albany; first run in 1975.

name: Northeast Regional (Roanoke)
highlight: From Boston down the whole Northeast Corridor, then past Washington by Charlottesville and Lynchburg to Roanoke, where the Northeast Regional, paid for by Virginia, brought trains back in 2017.
